articles.title: NEWS2ACTION: Improving timely sepsis care with a NEWS2-triggered Sepsis Code

affiliations.text: Department of Emergency Medicine, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.
Department of Infectious Diseases, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Sepsis requires early recognition, coordinated treatment, and rapid reassessment. A baseline review in our emergency department identified substantial delays in antimicrobial administration and delivery of other components of the Sepsis Six bundle, including among patients with marked physiological derangement.

abstract.heading: Objective
abstract.text: To evaluate whether a NEWS2-triggered Sepsis Code could improve the timely delivery of Sepsis Six-aligned bundle care and facilitate measurable and early physiological improvement.

abstract.heading: Methods
abstract.text: This single-center before-and-after clinical quality-improvement study compared a three-month pre-implementation period (October 1, 2025 - December 31, 2025) with a three-month post-implementation period (January 1, 2026 - March 31, 2026). The baseline cohort included 108 patients treated for suspected infection or sepsis, of whom 43 had NEWS2 ≥7. Following implementation, 39 consecutive patients with suspected infections and NEWS2 ≥7 triggered the Sepsis Code. The primary comparison was one-hour intravenous antimicrobial and other Sepsis Six bundle administration in the high-risk cohorts (43 before vs 39 after implementation). Post-code process times and repeat NEWS2 at 30 minutes were also evaluated.

abstract.heading: Results
abstract.text: One-hour antimicrobial administration increased from 16/43 (37.2%) before implementation to 39/39 (100%) after implementation (P < 0.001). Among patients triggering the Sepsis Code, the median times from emergency department arrival to code activation were 6 minutes, to laboratory testing and lactate assessment 16 minutes, to blood culture collection 18 minutes, and to antimicrobial administration 24 minutes. Mean NEWS2 decreased from 10.33 ± 2.13 to 6.77 ± 1.94 at 30 minutes, representing a mean reduction of 3.56 points (P < 0.001). NEWS2 decreased in 36/39 patients (92.3%), and 18/39 (46.2%) moved out of the high-risk category.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Implementation of a NEWS2-triggered Sepsis Code was associated with marked improvement in one-hour antimicrobial administration and delivery of other Sepsis Six-aligned bundle components, while establishing a structured 30-minute physiological reassessment point. Larger prospective studies are needed to assess the sustainability of these improvements and their effects on risk-adjusted clinical outcomes.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.1 Its global burden remains substantial, with an estimated 48.9 million cases and 11 million sepsis-related deaths in 2017.2 Contemporary Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidance emphasizes immediate resuscitation and prompt antimicrobial therapy in septic shock and in patients with a high likelihood of sepsis, while also stressing ongoing diagnostic reassessment and antimicrobial stewardship.3

Timely administration of effective antimicrobials is an important treatment target in severe sepsis and septic shock. Observational studies and meta-analytic evidence link treatment delay with poorer outcomes, although the strength of this association varies by population, severity of illness, and the certainty of infection.4–8 Effective sepsis pathways therefore depend not only on recognition of suspected infection, but also on translating recognition into parallel, time-critical actions. Bundle-based programs, including the Sepsis Six Bundle, demonstrated the value of coordinated early care supported by measurable performance targets.9–11

The National Early Warning Score (NEWS) and its updated NEWS2 framework provide a standardized bedside assessment of respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen requirement, systolic blood pressure, pulse, consciousness/new confusion, and temperature.12,13 NEWS2 has demonstrated utility in identifying emergency-department patients with infection who are at increased risk of organ dysfunction and adverse outcomes.14,15 Serial NEWS2 assessment may also provide a practical measure of early physiological response to treatment. In a large sepsis cohort, improvement in NEWS2 during emergency-department care was associated with lower hospital mortality.16

Our baseline process review suggested that clinically reasonable but sequential workflows were allowing small delays to accumulate. We therefore developed NEWS2ACTION, in which suspected infection with a NEWS2 ≥7 activates a shared Sepsis Code, coordinated Sepsis Six-aligned management, and repeat NEWS2 assessment at 30 minutes. This study evaluated the effect of that pathway on antimicrobial timing and early physiological response.

Methodology

Study design and setting

We conducted a single-center, before-and-after clinical quality-improvement study in the emergency department of KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum. The pre-implementation period was October 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025, and the post-implementation period was January 1, 2026 to March 31, 2026.

Participants

The baseline cohort comprised 108 patients assessed for suspected infection or sepsis who subsequently received antimicrobial therapy. NEWS2 was not an entry criterion during this period; 43 of the 108 patients had NEWS2 ≥7. After implementation, the Sepsis Code was activated for patients with suspected infection and a NEWS2 ≥7. The post-implementation cohort comprised 39 consecutive patients who triggered the Sepsis Code, all of whom were subsequently clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The principal before-and-after comparison was therefore restricted to the comparable high-risk cohorts: 43 patients before implementation and 39 patients after implementation.

Intervention

NEWS2ACTION used NEWS2 ≥7 as the institutional trigger for Sepsis Code activation. Operational principles included early recognition, rapid activation, parallel treatment, and objective reassessment. Following activation, laboratory testing, lactate assessment, blood cultures, empirical intravenous antimicrobials, hemodynamic assessment and indicated fluid therapy, oxygen or ventilatory support, urine-output assessment, vasopressors, and other organ support were initiated as clinically appropriate. The intervention was aligned with contemporary sepsis guidance and the Sepsis Six bundle concept.3,11 Bundle completion was clinician-led rather than automatic; interventions such as oxygen, fluid bolus, or catheterization were undertaken only when clinically indicated.

Outcomes and data collection

The primary process endpoint was administration of intravenous antimicrobial and other indicated bundle components within one hour of emergency-department arrival among patients with NEWS2 ≥7.

Post-code data included emergency-department arrival time, initial NEWS2, time to code activation, laboratory and lactate assessment, blood-culture collection, and antimicrobial administration, as well as oxygen or ventilatory support, intravenous fluid administration, vasopressor use, repeat NEWS2 at 30 minutes, risk-category migration, and available follow-up outcomes. The principal physiological endpoint was change in NEWS2 from activation to 30 minutes.

Data analysis and governance

Categorical data are presented as number (percentage), and continuous data as mean ± standard deviation or median, as available in the source dataset. The original analysis reported P < 0.001 for the high-risk pre-implementation vs post-implementation comparison of one-hour antimicrobial administration and for the change in NEWS2 at 30 minutes.

Results

Baseline antimicrobial timing

In the baseline cohort of 108 patients (pre-implementation), 34 (31.5%) received antimicrobials within 1 hour, 51 (47.2%) between 1 and 3 hours, and 23 (21.3%) after more than 3 hours. Within the high-risk subgroup with NEWS2 ≥7, only 16/43 (37.2%) received antimicrobials within 1 hour.

Speed of sepsis code delivery

Among the 39 patients who triggered the Sepsis Code, the median time from emergency-department arrival to code activation was 6 minutes. Laboratory testing and lactate assessment occurred at a median of 16 minutes, blood culture collection at 18 minutes, and intravenous antimicrobial administration at 24 minutes. Thirty-one of 39 patients (79.5%) received antimicrobials within 30 minutes, and all 39 (100%) received them within 60 minutes.

Early physiological response

Mean NEWS2 decreased from 10.33 ± 2.13 at activation to 6.77 ± 1.94 at 30 minutes, a mean reduction of 3.56 points (P < 0.001). Thirty-six patients (92.3%) had a lower NEWS2, two (5.1%) were unchanged, and one (2.6%) increased. All 39 patients triggered the Sepsis Code with a NEWS2 ≥7. At 30 minutes, 18/39 (46.2%) had moved out of the high-risk category: 14 were in the medium-risk category and 4 in the low-risk category, while 21 remained in the high-risk category.

Primary before-and-after comparison

Among comparable high-risk patients with NEWS2 ≥7, one-hour antimicrobial administration increased from 16/43 (37.2%) before implementation to 39/39 (100%) after implementation, an absolute increase of 62.8 percentage points (P < 0.001).

Discussion

The principal finding was a large improvement in reliability of one-hour antimicrobial delivery after implementing NEWS2ACTION. Restricting the main comparison to NEWS2 ≥7 patients reduced the most obvious baseline/post-code selection mismatch: 37.2% of high-risk patients received antimicrobials within one hour before the code compared with 100% after implementation. The median post-code antimicrobial time of 24 minutes suggests a workflow change beyond simply meeting the one-hour target.

The mechanism is operationally plausible. Before implementation, assessment, investigation, review, prescription, preparation, and administration often occurred sequentially. NEWS2ACTION attached a shared response to an objective physiological trigger and allowed several tasks to proceed in parallel. This aligns with the broader principle underlying bundle-based sepsis programs.9–11 NEWS2 served as both an activation trigger and a structured reassessment tool, while treatment remained individualized according to clinical need and current sepsis guidance.3,13

The early fall in NEWS2 is clinically encouraging but should not be interpreted as proof of improved survival. NEWS2 is a composite physiological score and can change rapidly with oxygenation, circulation, temperature, and consciousness. Serial NEWS2 therefore provides a useful direction-of-travel signal, consistent with prior work linking score improvement during emergency-department management with better outcomes.16 Likewise, lactate kinetics have been associated with prognosis in sepsis and support the broader concept of early objective reassessment.17 Early-warning-score-based clinical decision support has also shown potential to improve sepsis care processes and resource outcomes.18 Comparative studies have generally found NEWS2 to be at least as useful as qSOFA for identifying deterioration among infected patients, supporting its role as an operational trigger in settings where it is routinely measured.19,20

This study has important limitations. It was a single-center before-and-after quality-improvement evaluation with a small post-code cohort. Mortality, length of stay, source control, antimicrobial appropriateness, de-escalation, serial lactate, SOFA score, intensive-care use, and mechanical ventilation were not prospectively standardized as study outcomes. The observed reduction in NEWS2 therefore demonstrates early physiological improvement.

Future evaluation should prospectively enroll a larger post-code cohort, maintain uniform outcome definitions, assess protocol adherence and antimicrobial appropriateness, and include risk-adjusted 7-day and 28-day outcomes. Sustainability will also depend on staff education, simulation-based Sepsis Code drills, and periodic audit of process timestamps. Persistent or rising NEWS2 at 30 minutes may be particularly useful as a predefined trigger for senior reassessment and critical-care escalation.

Conclusion

Implementing a NEWS2-triggered Sepsis Code was associated with marked improvement in one-hour antimicrobial administration and delivery of other bundle components among high-risk emergency department patients and created a reproducible 30-minute physiological reassessment point. The intervention converted an early-warning score into a coordinated response through rapid activation, parallel treatment, communication, and structured reassessment. Larger prospective studies are required to determine sustainability, antimicrobial appropriateness, and effects on risk-adjusted patient outcomes.

articles.title: Progressive spastic paraparesis in a middle-aged male: A diagnostic challenge

affiliations.text: Department of Neurology, KIMSHEALTH, Kottayam, Kerala, India.

abstract.text: Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) is a rare neurodegenerative disorder that causes selective deterioration of the upper motor neurons (UMNs), with relative sparing of the lower motor neuron (LMN) system.^1,2^ The clinical course is characterized by progressive motor disability due to muscle spasticity, which typically involves the lower extremities and bulbar muscles. Here, we present a rare case of spastic, asymmetric paraparesis in a 62-year-old male in whom there was a diagnostic challenge.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

The prevalence of PLS is estimated to be around 2-3% of total cases of motor neuron disease (MND).

Conventionally, motor neuron disease comprises a clinical spectrum ranging from exclusively lower motor neuron (LMN) disease, as seen in progressive muscular atrophy, to purely upper motor neuron (UMN) disease, as seen in primary lateral sclerosis (PLS). In the broad middle exists amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which affects both UMNs and LMNs.

PLS, therefore, by definition, manifests as pure UMN disease/dysfunction (PUMND) from onset throughout the disease course. However, as most neuromuscular disease experts recognize, LMN disease/dysfunction (LMND) may sometimes develop in patients with a well-established diagnosis of PLS after many years.3

Case history

A 62-year-old male with a previous history of coronary artery disease, on medical management, presented with stiffness of both lower limbs for 8 months and difficulty in walking for 8 months.

He was apparently normal before presentation. His symptoms started as asymmetric stiffness of both lower limbs, with an insidious onset and progressive course, more pronounced in the left lower limb.

He noticed dragging of both feet and experienced multiple episodes of tripping. He described his legs as being very heavy, "like a log of wood". He also had mild difficulty getting up from a seated posture, mainly due to stiffness.

There was no history of wasting, cramps, fasciculations, or spasms. There were no upper-limb or craniobulbar symptoms. There were also no autonomic or extrapyramidal symptoms.

General examination

The patient was clinically stable, with normal vital signs. There was no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing or pedal edema. His Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30.

Cranial nerve examination was normal, with specifically no evidence of tongue wasting or fasciculations.

On examination of the motor system, muscle bulk was preserved. Grade 2 bilateral lower-limb spasticity was present. Power was normal in the neck and upper limbs (5/5), while power in the lower limbs was approximately 4+/5.

The abdominal reflexes were preserved. Plantar responses were bilaterally extensor. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk in both upper limbs, with biceps, triceps, and supinator reflexes graded as 3+ bilaterally. Knee jerks were 3+ bilaterally, more pronounced on the left, while ankle jerks were 4+ bilaterally. Subtle pyramidal signs were present in the upper limbs. A palmomental reflex was also present.

Coordination was normal in the upper limbs. Lower-limb coordination could not be adequately assessed because of marked spasticity.

Gait examination revealed a severe spastic gait with a narrow base. No fasciculations were observed. Sensory examination was normal. Examination of the skull and spine was unremarkable, and there was no peripheral nerve thickening.

Investigations

Routine laboratory investigations were largely unremarkable. Hemoglobin was 13.6 g/dL, total leukocyte count was 9,300/mm3, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 27 mm in the first hour.

Serum vitamin B12 was 635 pg/mL and serum copper was 81.5 μg/dL (reference range 70-140 μg/dL). Serum homocysteine was 14.8, within the stated reference range of less than 15. Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 3.4 mIU/mL. Viral markers were negative.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed no cells, with a glucose level of 78 mg% and protein level of 28 mg%. Culture and sensitivity showed no growth, and the sample was sterile.

Serological testing for human T-cell lymphotropic virus types 1 and 2 (HTLV-I/2) and anti-GAD65 antibodies was negative. Tumor markers were also negative.

Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed grade 1 fatty liver.

Nerve conduction study and electrophysiological studies

Sensory nerve action potentials were normal. Motor nerve conduction studies showed bilateral mild carpal tunnel syndrome, while the other studied nerves were normal.

Neuroimaging

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical and thoracic spine showed no significant abnormality or evidence of compressive pathology (Figure 1).

MRI of the brain, including T1-weighted and FLAIR sequences, was also normal (Figure 2).

Discussion and conclusion

The patient was evaluated as a case of pure UMN syndrome, predominantly affecting the lower limbs. Clinical examination revealed bipyramidal dysfunction.

Brain and spinal cord imaging was normal, with no evidence of compression.

Non-compressive myelopathy, including vitamin B12 deficiency, copper deficiency and other tractopathies, was considered. Infectious myelitis, including HIV, syphilis and HTLV infection, was also considered. Hereditary spastic paraplegia was considered, although the relatively late age of presentation and normal MRI findings made this less typical.

Other diagnostic possibilities included a pure UMN variant of motor neuron disease, particularly primary lateral sclerosis; toxic myelopathy; primary progressive multiple sclerosis; and stiff-leg syndrome within the stiff-person spectrum.

All routine biochemical tests, including vitamin B12 and homocysteine, and CSF studies were normal. Anti-GAD65 levels were also normal.

EMG showed a normal study of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar segments.

No spontaneous potential or gross denervation changes could be recorded from either of these segments. Hence, a provisional clinical diagnosis of primary lateral sclerosis was made. The patient was started on baclofen, diazepam and riluzole, along with physiotherapy for spasticity.

He remains under follow-up.

PLS is diagnosed by exclusion and is therefore challenging because the initial differential diagnosis is broad. This includes conditions such as metabolic myelopathies, including adrenomyeloneuropathy; primary progressive multiple sclerosis; Alexander disease; autoimmune diseases, such as those associated with anti-amphiphysin antibodies; infections, including human T-lymphotropic virus types 1 and 2 and syphilis; and paraneoplastic syndromes, for example in patients with breast cancer.

Most conditions in this differential diagnosis can be demonstrated through imaging, genetic and laboratory testing.2,1,3

articles.title: Agenesis of the ductus venosus with extrahepatic drainage into the inferior vena cava: Prenatal diagnosis and outcome

affiliations.text: Department of Maternal Fetal Medicine, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Agenesis of the ductus venosus (ADV) is a rare fetal vascular anomaly with a variable prognosis depending on the pattern of umbilical venous drainage. Extrahepatic drainage may result in significant cardiac volume overload and fetal compromise.

abstract.heading: Case
abstract.text: A 28-year-old gravida 3, para 0 (G3P0) with two previous missed miscarriages was diagnosed with ADV at 20 weeks gestation. The umbilical vein drained directly into a prominent inferior vena cava, with associated cardiomegaly, fused E/A waves, and an abnormal Tei index. Multiple hepatic calcifications were also noted, without other structural anomalies. Chromosomal microarray and whole-exome sequencing were normal. Despite the absence of genetic or major structural abnormalities, follow-up assessment at 23 weeks demonstrated progressive cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion, and generalized edema, consistent with hydrops fetalis. Following multidisciplinary counseling, the pregnancy was terminated because of progressive cardiac dysfunction and poor prognosis.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Isolated ADV with extrahepatic umbilical venous drainage can result in severe fetal hemodynamic compromise despite a normal genetic evaluation. Careful assessment of the drainage pathway, portal venous anatomy, cardiac function, and associated anomalies, together with close serial surveillance, is essential for prognostic counseling and timely management.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

The ductus venosus (DV) is a vital shunt in the fetal circulatory system, channeling 20-30% of oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein (UV) directly to the inferior vena cava (IVC) and heart, bypassing the hepatic circulation.1–4 Its presence ensures efficient delivery of oxygenated blood to the fetal brain and heart. Agenesis of the ductus venosus (ADV) is a rare vascular anomaly with a prevalence of 1:500 to 1:2500, in which this shunt fails to develop, resulting in alternative venous pathways such as intrahepatic or extrahepatic drainage of the umbilical vein.5 The condition may occur in isolation or be associated with chromosomal abnormalities, structural malformations, or other vascular anomalies. Prenatal diagnosis, typically by targeted fetal echocardiography or Doppler ultrasound, is important to assess the hemodynamic impact, identify associated anomalies, and guide perinatal management. Prognosis varies widely, depending on the pattern of umbilical venous drainage and the presence of comorbid conditions.6

Case description

A 28-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 0, with two prior missed miscarriages, presented for a targeted anomaly scan at 20 weeks' gestation. Her first-trimester ultrasound at 12 + 5 weeks demonstrated normal nuchal translucency and nasal bone, with no structural abnormalities. Combined first-trimester screening indicated low risk for common aneuploidies.

At 20 weeks, ultrasound revealed normal fetal biometry, amniotic fluid index, and umbilical artery Doppler. Detailed fetal echocardiography showed normal cardiac and abdominal situs with no structural cardiac defects. However, the DV was not visualized, and the umbilical vein drained directly into a prominent IVC. Cardiomegaly was noted, with evolving cardiac dysfunction evidenced by fused E/A waves and an abnormal Tei index. Multiple subdiaphragmatic hepatic calcifications were identified. No extracardiac anomalies were detected. The normal and abnormal drainage of the umbilical vein (UV) images are shown in Figures 1-3.

A multidisciplinary team comprising an obstetrician, maternal-fetal medicine specialist, geneticist, and neonatologist provided counseling. Invasive genetic testing was performed, and both chromosomal microarray and whole-exome sequencing were normal. A diagnosis of isolated ADV with extrahepatic drainage of the umbilical vein into the IVC and hepatic calcifications was made.

The parents were counseled regarding the guarded prognosis and opted for re-evaluation in three weeks. At 23 weeks, follow-up ultrasound demonstrated worsening cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion, and generalized edema, indicating evolving hydrops fetalis. Given the poor prognosis, the parents and multidisciplinary team made a shared decision to terminate the pregnancy.

This case illustrates that even in the absence of genetic or extracardiac anomalies, isolated ADV with extrahepatic umbilical venous drainage can lead to progressive cardiac dysfunction and an adverse perinatal outcome.

Discussion

Management of absent ductus venosus involves detailed prenatal assessment and close surveillance to determine the drainage pattern, associated anomalies, and hemodynamic impact. Targeted Doppler and fetal echocardiography should assess the umbilical and portal venous systems, cardiac anatomy and function, and associated structural or chromosomal abnormalities.7 Serial ultrasound is recommended to monitor fetal growth, cardiac function, amniotic fluid volume, polyhydramnios, and to detect evolving complications such as high-output cardiac failure and hydrops fetalis. Genetic testing should be considered, particularly when additional anomalies or sonographic markers are present.

When continuation of pregnancy is appropriate, delivery should be planned in a tertiary care center with neonatal intensive care (NICU) and pediatric cardiology support. The timing and mode of delivery should be based on fetal and obstetric indications. Postnatally, neonatal echocardiography and evaluation of the portal venous system are recommended, along with monitoring for cardiac failure, pulmonary hypertension, hypoglycemia, and liver dysfunction.8,9 Stable isolated cases may be managed conservatively, while symptomatic portosystemic shunts or significant cardiac/metabolic complications may require targeted intervention.10

Conclusion

Agenesis of the ductus venosus with extrahepatic umbilical venous drainage is rare, and its hemodynamic impact depends on the site of umbilical vein drainage, the presence and integrity of the portal venous system, associated portosystemic shunts, and the resultant cardiac volume load. A thorough evaluation for associated structural and chromosomal abnormalities is essential, with genetic testing considered when clinically indicated. Serial ultrasound and Doppler surveillance are important for early identification of evolving fetal hemodynamic compromise. Even in apparently isolated cases, extrahepatic drainage may be associated with adverse perinatal outcomes, as illustrated by the present case, warranting close antenatal surveillance and timely intervention.

abstract.text: Intravenous iron sucrose is often perceived as a safer alternative to ferric carboxymaltose but can induce severe symptomatic hypophosphatemia. We report the case of a 44-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia whose fatigue and dyspnea worsened despite a successful hemoglobin response following iron sucrose infusion. This led to testing her phosphate levels, and she was found to have profound hypophosphatemia (1.4 mg/dL) alongside an inappropriately non-suppressed fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) level. She was successfully treated with phosphate repletion and cholecalciferol. This case challenges the perception of iron sucrose as uniquely safe and underscores the need for clinicians to monitor phosphate levels, particularly after multi-dose regimens, and to consider hypophosphatemia in patients with persistent or worsening symptoms following otherwise successful intravenous (IV) iron therapy.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is a major global health concern, affecting an estimated one-third of the world's population and disproportionately affecting women of reproductive age and individuals with chronic diseases. For patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to oral iron, or for those requiring rapid repletion, intravenous iron therapy is a standard and highly effective treatment.1

Hypophosphatemia is a recognized adverse effect of IV iron therapy. Initially and most prominently reported with ferric carboxymaltose (FCM), this complication was often regarded as a distinctive drawback of this formulation.2 This perception was reinforced by randomized controlled trials that demonstrated a significantly higher incidence of hypophosphatemia with FCM (74-78%) compared to iron isomaltoside (0-8%).3 Consequently, iron sucrose has often been considered a safer alternative with respect to this complication. Emerging evidence now challenges this notion, confirming that the propensity to induce hypophosphatemia is an inherent characteristic of IV iron therapy as a class. However, its incidence and severity vary among preparations. The pathophysiology is rooted in the administration of IV iron itself, which stimulates the production of the phosphaturic hormone fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23).4

Case presentation

A 44-year-old premenopausal woman presented to the emergency department with profound fatigue and occasional dyspnoea on mild exertion. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, a previous Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA), significant left Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) stenosis, and dyslipidemia. Following her TIA, she was placed on dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with Clopidogrel and Aspirin. She had a history of severe menorrhagia with passage of clots for 3 years, which had developed after initiation of DAPT. She was referred to the hematology outpatient department for evaluation of anemia.

A comprehensive hematological evaluation was performed. A conventional coagulation panel was done because of menorrhagia, and was normal. Red blood cell indices showed a microcytic pattern, confirmed by peripheral blood film revealing hypochromic, microcytic red blood cells, consistent with iron deficiency. The reticulocyte count was low at 1.18%, indicating an inadequate bone marrow response. Iron studies showed depleted ferritin (12.5 μg/L), low serum iron (30 μg/dL), and elevated total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) (434.5 μg/dL), resulting in a profoundly low transferrin saturation of 6.8%. This biochemical profile confirmed severe iron deficiency anemia. She was started on a course of IV iron sucrose, receiving four infusions of 200 mg each on alternate days. Following completion of therapy, her haemoglobin increased to 12.8 g/dL, indicating a successful haematological response.

Despite correction of her anemia, she subsequently returned to the clinic with worsening fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. Her vital signs were stable with normal oxygen tension in ambient air, and her ECG and troponin levels were normal. The laboratory workup during this admission revealed severe hypophosphatemia, with a serum phosphorus level of 1.4 mg/dL. However, the random urine phosphorus level was lower (16.7 mg/dL). IV iron sucrose-associated hypophosphatemia was considered the most likely diagnosis.

Serum fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) concentration was within the high-normal range at 75.71 RU/mL (reference range: 23.20-95.40 RU/mL), despite profound hypophosphatemia, which should normally suppress FGF23 production entirely. Further metabolic workup revealed a decreased vitamin D level of 28.3 ng/mL, indicating insufficiency, while serum calcium and magnesium levels were within normal limits.

Although hypophosphatemia is reported more frequently and prominently with ferric carboxymaltose (FCM), severe hypophosphatemia can rarely occur following iron sucrose administration. Concomitant vitamin D insufficiency, along with elevated FGF23, may have contributed to the development or persistence of hypophosphatemia in this patient. This complication is important to recognize in the era of parenteral iron therapy.

In view of her symptoms and the severity of hypophosphatemia, acute phosphate replacement was initiated. For acute IV repletion, she received an intravenous infusion of potassium phosphate. She was transitioned to oral phosphate supplementation with potassium phosphate sachets three times daily. A repeat serum phosphorus level improved to 2.2 mg/dL following initial treatment. Given her concomitant vitamin D insufficiency, she was also prescribed weekly cholecalciferol to address potential contributory factors to bone metabolism and facilitate phosphate absorption. The patient reported significant improvement in her symptoms, with resolution of dyspnea and tiredness within 48 hours of initiating therapy. She was discharged with close outpatient follow-up.

Discussion

The pathophysiology of hypophosphatemia following intravenous (IV) iron therapy centers on FGF23, a hormone produced predominantly by osteocytes that regulates phosphate and vitamin D metabolism.4 Its physiological actions include promoting phosphaturia by downregulating sodium-phosphate cotransporters in the renal proximal tubule and suppressing the conversion of vitamin D to its active form, calcitriol. Intravenous iron administration triggers a rapid and sustained increase in levels of intact biologically active FGF23, likely stimulated by the sudden surge in bioavailable iron. In this case, the pretreatment iron studies confirmed severe deficiency, and the post-treatment hematological response confirmed effective repletion. An inappropriately high normal FGF23 level during this episode of severe hypophosphatemia may be proof of this mechanism.

The development of severe symptomatic hypophosphatemia after a multi-dose course of iron sucrose is consistent with emerging evidence that this complication can occur with other IV iron formulations. The onset of symptoms following the fourth infusion suggests the documented cumulative dose-effect relationship on FGF23 production. The patient's symptoms of fatigue and dyspnea, which persisted after a successful hematological response (Hb 10.2 g/dL), are a classic red flag for iatrogenic hypophosphatemia. This is a critical diagnostic pitfall, as these symptoms can mimic anemia and be misattributed to treatment failure.

This case has several implications for clinical practice. Iron sucrose should not be assumed to be free of clinically significant effects on phosphate metabolism, as all IV iron formulations carry this risk. Clinicians should actively monitor serum phosphate levels before starting IV iron therapy and again 1-2 weeks after completing a course, particularly in patients receiving multiple doses or with preexisting risk factors. There is need for more awareness to be raised among both patients and clinicians about the nonspecific symptoms of hypophosphatemia. This can lead to early diagnosis and intervention. Management involves phosphate repletion, with IV therapy reserved for severe or symptomatic cases. However, because the primary driver is renal wasting, supplementation can be challenging and requires close monitoring to avoid both undertreatment and the risks associated with overtreatment, such as hypocalcemia and metastatic calcification.5

Conclusion

The key take-home message is the need for heightened vigilance. As the use of intravenous iron therapy continues to increase, hypophosphatemia should be considered a potential complication, even with formulations such as iron sucrose that are generally perceived to carry a lower risk. Close monitoring, a high index of clinical suspicion, and timely recognition and management are essential to prevent morbidity and optimize the safety and effectiveness of IV iron therapy.

abstract.heading: Introduction
abstract.text: Cryptococcosis is a life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection caused by *Cryptococcus neoformans*. Primary cutaneous cryptococcosis (PCC) is a distinct clinical entity resulting from direct percutaneous inoculation.^1,2^ Although it is a recognized cause of localized infection in immunocompetent individuals, PCC is exceptionally rare in immunocompromised patients, in whom disseminated disease is more common. In solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients, cryptococcosis typically develops within the first two years following transplantation, during periods of intense immunosuppression. Late-onset presentation occurring after a decade of graft stability is uncommon and may pose a significant diagnostic challenge.^1^ Furthermore, a herpetiform presentation of PCC can create a significant diagnostic masquerade, potentially resulting in delays in appropriate therapy.

This is a case of a 48-year-old woman who presented 14 years after renal transplantation with a background of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and hypertension, and a one-day history of grouped, fluid-filled herpetiform lesions over the right forearm. Given the clinical morphology and her immunocompromised status, herpesvirus infection was initially suspected, and she was treated with acyclovir. However, a negative Tzanck smear and lack of clinical improvement prompted diagnostic reassessment. Over the next five days, the cutaneous lesions evolved into necrotic pustules and ulcers, accompanied by significant ipsilateral lymphadenopathy. A thorough history later revealed a thorn prick while gardening, suggesting direct inoculation as the likely route. Skin biopsy and fungal culture confirmed cryptococcosis caused by *Cryptococcus deneoformans*. A comprehensive evaluation for systemic involvement, including pulmonary imaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, was negative, confirming primary cutaneous cryptococcosis with lymphangitic spread. Targeted systemic antifungal therapy led to complete resolution of the cutaneous lesions, with healing and atrophic scarring.

articles.bodyHtml:
Case report

A 48-year-old woman from Trivandrum, who had undergone renal transplantation in 2012, presented to the outpatient department with clear, fluid-filled lesions over the right forearm of one day's duration, associated with a burning sensation. She had maintained stable graft function for 14 years. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. She was receiving tacrolimus and prednisolone; mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) had subsequently been replaced with azathioprine. She reported an episode of fever and abdominal pain a few days before presentation. There was no history of similar lesions elsewhere, recent travel, or recent changes in medication.

Dermatological examination

Dermatological examination revealed multiple grouped and discrete, clear, fluid-filled vesicles with a herpetiform distribution over the right forearm near the elbow, on a minimally erythematous background (Figure 1). Given the patient's immunosuppressed status and lesion morphology, herpes simplex virus (HSV) was the most likely diagnosis.

A Tzanck smear was performed, and the patient was started on oral acyclovir 200 mg twice daily, with the dose selected in view of her elevated serum creatinine (7.6 mg/dL), along with topical acyclovir cream three times daily for one week.

On day 5, the patient returned with no clinical improvement and worsening pain. Vesicles had evolved into pustules and necrotic areas. A repeat Tzanck smear showed sheets of neutrophils and a few acantholytic cells, but no multinucleated giant cells.

On examination at this stage, multiple, discrete, small (pinhead-sized), non-follicular, creamy-yellow pustules were scattered over an erythematous base on the flexural aspect of the forearm. In the central area, several pustules had coalesced to form larger lakes of pus, with yellowish-brown and hemorrhagic crusting overlying the central area (Figures 2 and 3). Edema of the right upper limb and ipsilateral right axillary lymphadenopathy were present.

A non-healing ulcer on the right index finger was noted accidentally (Figure 4). Further history revealed that the patient had sustained a thorn prick while gardening, which she initially considered insignificant. This was followed by an unsuccessful incision and drainage procedure at a local hospital.

The thorn prick was considered the likely site of direct inoculation.

Around the same time, facial lesions also developed. These consisted of:

  1. Multiple grouped, well-circumscribed, umbilicated papules and pseudovesicles over the right perioral region near the nasolabial fold. The lesions appeared succulent and fleshy, with central umbilication; some showed yellow crusting and minor erosions on the right perioral area near the nasolabial fold (Figure 5).
  2. A single well-defined umbilicated papule over the left cheek.

Differential diagnosis

  1. Based on the evolution and morphology of the lesions in an immunocompromised patient, the differential diagnoses included: deep fungal infections, particularly cryptococcosis and sporotrichosis.
  2. Pyoderma gangrenosum
  3. Atypical mycobacterial infection

Laboratory and histopathological evaluation

Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 17,500 cells/mm3, C-reactive protein of 304 mg/L, and serum creatinine of 8 mg/dL. Gram staining of the lymph node tissue showed no organisms, and MTB GeneXpert was negative. Blood cultures were sterile.

Histopathological examination of the skin biopsy showed dense nodular suppurative inflammation with a mixed lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate. Foci of granulomatous inflammation comprising epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells were also present. Numerous encapsulated rounded yeast forms were seen in groups. The yeasts exhibited prominent pericellular halos, with some showing a bilaminar appearance (Figure 6). On Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining, the fungal elements stained jet black against a pale green to bluish background (Figure 7). Mucicarmine staining highlighted the acidic mucopolysaccharide capsule, which stained a vibrant pink color (Figure 8). Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining demonstrated fungal cell walls as bright magenta-purple structures (Figure 9).

Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) produced creamy, glistening, highly mucoid colonies, consistent with a thick polysaccharide capsule (Figure 10).

The skin biopsy was reported as showing Cryptococcus, while tissue biopsy demonstrated cryptococcal-like fungal elements.

Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) identified the organism as Cryptococcus deneoformans.

Serum cryptococcal antigen was negative. CT imaging of the chest & head showed no significant abnormality apart from pleural effusion. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed no sign of infection; CSF cryptococcal antigen was negative, and India ink staining was also negative. These findings, together with the absence of pulmonary or CNS involvement, supported a diagnosis of primary cutaneous cryptococcosis.

Final diagnosis

A diagnosis of primary cutaneous cryptococcosis caused by Cryptococcus deneoformans in an immunocompromised host, with lymphangitic spread, was made.

The patient was treated with intravenous conventional amphotericin B at a dose of 50 mg/day for 14 days, along with flucytosine 1250 mg every 48 hours.

Discussion

Primary cutaneous cryptococcosis is a rare condition characterized by localized skin eruptions with no evidence of systemic involvement.1,2 It is caused by fungi of the genus Cryptococcus - C. neoformans / C. deneoformans.3 It occurs when the fungus is inoculated directly into the skin through a traumatic injury - like our patient's thorn prick - introducing the fungus into the dermis from environmental sources such as soil or bird droppings. It manifests most commonly as papules, ulcers, or cellulitis; an initial presentation with vesicles is uncommon.4,5

The case highlights that, in transplant recipients, initial grouped "vesicle-like" lesions are not always herpes; they can be a "sentinel" (the first warning sign) of a potentially life-threatening fungal infection.

This case adds to the limited literature on 'sporotrichoid' cryptococcosis, emphasizing that environmental inoculation can mimic traditional 'rose gardener's disease' in high-risk patients.

In immunocompromised patients, the skin can provide a window for early diagnosis. By identifying the "sentinel" skin lesions through biopsy, we were able to establish the diagnosis and initiate appropriate treatment.

PCC is more commonly described in immunocompetent individuals, making its occurrence as a localized cutaneous and lymphatic infection in an immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient particularly unusual.

The case also presented a diagnostic dilemma between an infectious and an inflammatory process. The ulceration following the thorn prick and the history of an unsuccessful incision and drainage procedure raised the possibility of pyoderma gangrenosum. However, biopsy resolved the dilemma and helped avoid potentially inappropriate treatment with steroids.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Retrocaval ureter is a rare congenital vascular anomaly in which the ureter passes posterior to the inferior vena cava (IVC), potentially causing ureteric obstruction and hydronephrosis. Minimally invasive repair is increasingly preferred in suitable patients, with robotic surgery offering potential advantages in visualization, dissection, and intracorporeal suturing.

abstract.heading: Case presentation
abstract.text: An 18-year-old female undergoing evaluation for irregular menstrual cycles was incidentally found to have right hydronephrosis. She was asymptomatic, with no flank pain, voiding symptoms, or fever, and no history of abdominal or urological surgery. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable. The ureter was dilated up to the level of the L4 vertebra, where it deviated medially and coursed posterior to the IVC, confirming the diagnosis of right retrocaval ureter.

abstract.heading: Intervention
abstract.text: Robotic excision of the retrocaval segment with anterior repositioning and ureteroureterostomy was performed. The patient was placed in the left lateral position using a four-port robotic configuration. Following medial reflection of the colon and kocherization of the duodenum, the IVC and ureter were identified. The proximal and distal ureter were dissected while preserving the periureteral blood supply. The retrocaval segment was transected, and the ureter repositioned anterior to the IVC. A spatulated tension-free end-to-end ureteroureterostomy was then performed over a 6 Fr double-J stent using 3-0 Vicryl sutures.

abstract.heading: Outcome
abstract.text: Operative time was 96 minutes with minimal blood loss and no intraoperative complications. No drain was placed. The Foley catheter was removed on postoperative day 2, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. The double-J stent was removed at 6 weeks. The patient remains under follow-up.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: Robotic repair provides a safe, technically feasible minimally invasive option for retrocaval ureter. Enhanced visualization and wristed instrumentation facilitate precise ureteric dissection, anterior repositioning, and intracorporeal ureteroureterostomy.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Retrocaval ureter, also termed circumcaval ureter, is a rare congenital anomaly resulting from abnormal embryological development of the inferior vena cava (IVC). The ureter passes posterior to the IVC and may become compressed, resulting in varying degrees of proximal hydroureteronephrosis. The anomaly predominantly affects the right ureter because of the embryological development of the IVC. Although many patients are asymptomatic, obstruction may present with flank pain, recurrent urinary tract infection, or deterioration of renal drainage.1,2

Historically, open excision of the retrocaval segment followed by anterior repositioning and ureteroureterostomy was the standard treatment. Laparoscopic and robotic techniques have subsequently emerged as minimally invasive alternatives. Comparative data suggest that robotic reconstruction can reduce operative time while maintaining comparable perioperative outcomes.3,4

Case presentation

An 18-year-old female was evaluated for irregular menstrual cycles and was incidentally found to have right-sided hydronephrosis. She had no flank pain, dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or fever. There was no history of previous abdominal, pelvic, or urological surgery. On examination, the abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no palpable mass. Routine laboratory investigations were normal. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli, for which she received appropriate antibiotic treatment.

CT urography performed at an outside hospital in August 2025 demonstrated good contrast excretion from both kidneys. The right renal pelvicalyceal system and upper third of the ureter were dilated. The dilated right upper ureter was traced to approximately the L4 vertebral level, where it deviated medially and passed posterior to the IVC, a characteristic configuration confirming the diagnosis of a right retrocaval ureter. The left ureter and urinary bladder were normal. The imaging findings were particularly important for operative planning because they demonstrated the exact anatomical relationship between the ureter and the IVC before reconstruction.5

Despite the absence of symptoms, the presence of hydronephrosis and the abnormal obstructive course prompted consideration of reconstructive surgery. The patient underwent robotic repair after counselling regarding the nature of the anomaly, available treatment options, and the risks of reconstructive ureteric surgery.

Robotic surgical technique and postoperative course

The patient was placed in the left lateral position using a four-port robotic configuration. Following medial reflection of the colon and kocherization of the duodenum, the IVC and right ureter were clearly visualized. The proximal and distal ureter were dissected carefully with preservation of periureteral blood supply, and the retrocaval segment was mobilized. The key technical objective was to release the ureter from its retrocaval course while preserving its vascularity. After adequate mobilization, the abnormal retrocaval segment was excised, and the ureter was repositioned anterior to the IVC without tension. The ends were spatulated, and an intracorporeal end-to-end ureteroureterostomy was completed over a 6 Fr double-J stent using 3-0 Vicryl sutures. The use of robotic wristed instruments facilitated needle handling and precise suturing around the major vascular structure.3,4,6

The postoperative recovery was uncomplicated. There were no intraoperative complications and no drain was required. The Foley catheter was removed on postoperative day 2, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. The double-J stent was removed at 6 weeks postoperatively. At the time of this report, the patient remains asymptomatic on regular clinical follow-up.

Discussion

Retrocaval ureter is an uncommon congenital anomaly resulting from abnormal venous development, in which the ureter passes posterior to the IVC. Modern cross-sectional imaging has substantially improved preoperative diagnosis and anatomical definition. CT urography is particularly useful for demonstrating the characteristic ureteric course and associated hydronephrosis.1,5

Management depends on severity of symptoms, degree of obstruction, renal function, and the extent or progression of hydronephrosis. In patients requiring surgical reconstruction, the fundamental principles are excision of the compressed retrocaval segment, anterior repositioning of the ureter, and a tension-free ureteric anastomosis. Laparoscopic series have demonstrated favorable functional outcomes, while robotic surgery may facilitate intracorporeal suturing and dissection in this anatomically demanding location.4,7

The present case is notable because the patient was young and clinically asymptomatic, with the anomaly detected incidentally. The decision to proceed with reconstruction was based on the presence of hydronephrosis and the obstructive anatomical configuration. Previous reports have similarly described asymptomatic patients in whom retrocaval ureter was diagnosed incidentally on imaging.6,8

In a comparative study, Temiz et al. reported a mean operative time of 92 minutes for robotic repair compared with 190 minutes for laparoscopic repair, with broadly comparable blood loss, drain removal, and hospital stay.3 The operative time of 96 minutes in the present case is consistent with the reported efficiency of robotic reconstruction. A recent robot-assisted case report in a young woman also described successful reconstruction without perioperative complications and resolution of hydronephrosis on follow-up.6

The rarity of retrocaval ureter means that evidence remains predominantly based on case reports and small series. Therefore, the choice between laparoscopic and robotic approaches should be individualized based on surgeon experience, available technology, patient factors, and cost considerations.4,7

Conclusion

Robotic excision of the retrocaval ureteric segment with anterior repositioning and ureteroureterostomy is a safe and technically feasible minimally invasive procedure. In this young asymptomatic female with incidentally detected hydronephrosis, the procedure was completed in 96 minutes with minimal blood loss, no complications, and an uncomplicated early postoperative recovery. The case highlights the potential utility of robotic visualization in facilitating precise ureteric dissection, anterior repositioning, and intracorporeal ureteroureterostomy.

articles.title: Tirzepatide for obesity in a Class 1 commercial pilot with cardiometabolic risk: aeromedical considerations

abstract.text: Obesity and cardiometabolic disease present important challenges in aviation medicine because both the underlying conditions and their treatment may affect operational performance. This case report describes a 54-year-old Class 1 commercial pilot with obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, prediabetes, grade 3 hepatic steatosis, and a history of smoking who was removed from flight duties after admission in February 2026 with accelerated hypertension and troponin elevation. He reported no chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea, and clinical examination was unremarkable. ECG showed sinus rhythm without reported ischemic changes, while echocardiography and coronary angiography were normal. During a non-flying period, weekly tirzepatide was initiated alongside intensive cardiovascular risk-factor management and lifestyle modification. After approximately four months, he reported no treatment-related adverse effects. Blood pressure improved from 160/100 to 128/78 mmHg, BMI decreased from 37.3 to 33.5 kg/m^2^, and HbA1c was 5.8%. He remained asymptomatic, and cardiology considered him stable. However, clinical improvement alone does not establish fitness to fly. Return-to-flight assessment should consider cardiovascular presentation, functional capacity, medication stability, and tolerability, and the licensing requirements of the responsible aeromedical authority before certification.

Introduction

Obesity is a chronic condition associated with hypertension, dyslipidemia, impaired glucose regulation, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and other conditions relevant to occupational health.1 In commercial aviation, its significance extends beyond long-term morbidity, as disease-related symptoms, treatment effects, and functional limitations may impact safe cockpit performance. Aeromedical assessment must, therefore, consider not only the medical diagnosis but also the potential for subtle impairment during safety-critical tasks.

Tirzepatide is a once-weekly agent that acts as a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that can produce substantial weight loss and improve cardiometabolic outcomes in adults with obesity. Gastrointestinal adverse effects are most frequently reported during treatment initiation and dose escalation. Longer-term evidence in adults with obesity and prediabetes has demonstrated sustained weight loss and a reduced risk of progression to type 2 diabetes.2

However, evidence from the general clinical population cannot be directly translated into immediate fitness for flight. Adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased oral intake, dehydration, dizziness, and fatigue may have operational implications for pilots. Aeromedical assessment must therefore consider the underlying condition and indication for treatment, the medication's adverse-effect profile and tolerability, and the stability of the individual's clinical and functional status. Prescribed GLP-1 and combined GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists for obesity could be suitable for all classes of certification including Class 1, provided the user receives appropriate aeromedical assessment before starting and around dose changes.3 Prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists and combined GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists for obesity may be compatible with all classes of certification, including Class 1 certification, but require appropriate aeromedical assessment before treatment initiation and around dose adjustments.3

This case is of particular aeromedical interest because tirzepatide was initiated following a recent cardiovascular presentation characterized by accelerated hypertension and troponin elevation. Medication use was therefore not the only aeromedical question. The case describes the subsequent treatment response and the clinical and aeromedical considerations relevant to any potential return to flight operations. It follows the CARE case-report framework.

Case presentation

Patient and relevant background

The patient was a 54-year-old male commercial pilot who held a Class 1 medical certificate. Details of his licenses and airline affiliation are omitted to preserve confidentiality. He had a history of obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, prediabetes, and grade 3 hepatic steatosis. He had previously been a smoker and was using nicotine replacement therapy. His family history was negative for ischemic heart disease, stroke, or type 2 diabetes. Before his presentation in February 2026, he also had several modifiable lifestyle risk factors, including a poor diet, limited physical activity, and alcohol consumption of approximately 10-15 units per week.

The combination of obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, impaired glucose regulation, and previous smoking indicated a high cardiometabolic risk profile (Figure 1). In a professional pilot, these risk factors required attention because subsequent aeromedical disposition would need to establish that neither the underlying conditions nor their treatment resulted in symptoms, adverse effects, or functional limitations relevant to flight safety.4

February 2026 presentation

While still undertaking flight duties, the pilot was admitted in February 2026 with accelerated hypertension, with a blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg, with elevated troponin and D-dimer levels. He denied chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea and there were no abnormalities on cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examination. ECG showed no ischemic changes and was normal for sinus rhythm. Echocardiogram and coronary angiogram performed on February 15, 2026 were also reported as normal.

The treating team attributed the troponin elevation to uncontrolled hypertension. However, the available clinical records did not allow definitive classification of the troponin elevation as myocardial infarction or another specific acute coronary syndrome. This distinction was relevant to the subsequent aeromedical assessment and determination of Class 1 fitness (Figure 2).

Management and follow-up

Following the cardiovascular presentation, amlodipine/valsartan 10/160 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg, rosuvastatin 20 mg, ezetimibe 10 mg, aspirin 75 mg and metformin extended-release 1g were prescribed. The cardiologist subsequently recommended tirzepatide and intensive lifestyle changes. The pilot did not receive clearance to resume flying.5

He was subsequently removed from flight duties and remained in a period of ground duties and annual leave, resulting in no further flight exposure. Weekly tirzepatide was initiated during this non-flying period. This allowed potential early treatment-related effects, including gastrointestinal symptoms and reduced oral intake, to be observed while he remained off flight duties and during subsequent dose escalation. He had no flight exposure after the February 2026 presentation.

At follow-up, four months after the initial event in June 2026, the patient was on amlodipine/valsartan 10/160 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg, rosuvastatin 20 mg, ezetimibe 10 mg, aspirin 75 mg, and tirzepatide 7.5 mg once a week. Metformin was discontinued. He did not report any side effects from tirzepatide treatment. Nicotine replacement therapy was stopped, alcohol consumption had decreased to less than 10 units per week, and his diet had substantially improved, although physical activity remained limited (Figure 3).

Objective measures also improved. Blood pressure decreased to 128/78 mmHg, and BMI decreased from 37.3 to 33.5 kg/m2. HbA1c was 5.8%. The LDL value recorded was 131 mg/dl; however, the unit is not stated and is therefore not interpretable. ECG remained normal, and he reported no symptoms. Cardiology considered him clinically stable on the treatment regimen.

Despite these improvements, no final determination of Class 1 certification had been made. The clinical record indicated improvement, but the aeromedical certification required a separate assessment by the responsible licensing authority and evidence relevant to operational safety.

Discussion

This case illustrates the difference between effective treatment of obesity and demonstrated aeromedical fitness. The patient experienced early improvements in BMI, blood pressure, and glycaemic parameters after initiation of tirzepatide, without reported treatment-related adverse effects.6 However, these clinical improvements did not by themselves resolve the principal certification question: whether a commercial pilot with a recent presentation involving accelerated hypertension and troponin elevation could safely exercise license privileges.

The first consideration is the cardiovascular presentation. Although echocardiogram and coronary angiography were reported as normal, these investigations alone do not establish the mechanism of the troponin elevation or determine its aeromedical significance. The treating diagnosis, clinical course, blood pressure control, functional capacity, and any additional investigations required by the licensing authority remain relevant.7 The absence of chest pain and ischemic ECG changes provides useful clinical information. However, these findings must be interpreted in the context of the complete presentation rather than in isolation.

The second consideration is medication tolerability and stability. Tirzepatide is effective for weight management, but gastrointestinal side effects are common, especially during treatment initiation and dose escalation. Such effects may have operational implications for pilots through dehydration, reduced oral intake, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, or other symptoms that could interfere with concentration and performance. So the relevant question is not simply whether tirzepatide is an effective treatment, but whether the individual can take the medication at a stable dose without adverse effects that could compromise safe flight operations (Figure 4).

Treatment response was observed during a non-flying period, with no cockpit exposure after the February 2026 presentation. This was important because tirzepatide was subsequently titrated to a 7.5 mg once-weekly regimen. The absence of reported adverse effects approximately four months after treatment initiation was encouraging, but the date of the most recent dose escalation and the duration of stability at the maintenance dose should be documented before any return-to-duty assessment. Current UK Civil Aviation Authority guidance acknowledges the potential for gastrointestinal adverse effects during treatment initiation and dose escalation and incorporates clinical stability and appropriate aeromedical observation into certification considerations.8

The third consideration is the indication for treatment. Aeromedical assessment may differ depending on the underlying condition being treated, and tirzepatide may be prescribed for obesity or type 2 diabetes. Here, the patient had documented obesity and prediabetes, an HbA1c of 5.8% at follow-up, and a history of metformin discontinuation. Future emergence of diabetes may then need to be assessed using the applicable diabetes certification pathway.

The fourth consideration is comprehensive cardiometabolic risk management. Anti-obesity pharmacotherapy should complement, rather than replace, management of other modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking exposure, diet, alcohol consumption, and physical inactivity.9 In this case, blood pressure improved, nicotine replacement therapy was discontinued, alcohol consumption decreased, and dietary habits improved. Physical activity, however, remained limited, highlighting the need for continued lifestyle intervention and follow-up.

Evidence from obesity trials supports the clinical relevance of tirzepatide-associated weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic parameters.10 Cardiovascular benefits have also been demonstrated with incretin-based therapies in selected populations. However, evidence from these populations cannot automatically be extrapolated to an individual pilot's aeromedical fitness.11 Similarly, tirzepatide-associated weight loss may improve obstructive sleep apnea in patients with obesity. Still, obstructive sleep apnea was not documented in this patient and should not be inferred from the presence of obesity alone.12

Finally, this case highlights the importance of jurisdiction-specific aeromedical requirements. UK Civil Aviation Authority guidance indicates that GLP-1 receptor agonists and combined GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists used for obesity may be compatible with Class 1 certification; however, compatibility with certification does not automatically confer fitness to fly (Figure 5). The responsible aeromedical authority may require observation following treatment initiation, dose adjustment, and treatment interruption and restart (UK Civil Aviation Authority, 2026). Certification may also depend on the underlying cardiovascular diagnosis, relevant investigations, and specialist reports. In the same way, international aeromedical principles require license holders to be free from a disease or treatment effect that is likely to interfere with the safe exercise of license privileges.13,14

Aeromedical management considerations

The aeromedical implications of this case go beyond the reported clinical benefits of tirzepatide for weight reduction and cardiometabolic risk. Before any decision regarding return to flight, the responsible aeromedical authority should consider the underlying cardiovascular presentation, the indication for treatment, medication tolerability and stability, and whether the disease or its treatment could affect the pilot's ability to exercise license privileges safely.15 The principal considerations are summarized in Table 3.

These considerations support a holistic approach to aeromedical certification rather than one based solely on medication use or weight reduction. A return-to-flight decision should be taken only when cardiovascular risk has been assessed appropriately, cardiovascular management is stable and well tolerated, and there is no evidence that cardiovascular conditions or cardiovascular management is likely to affect the safe exercise of Class 1 license privileges.

Conclusion

In this 54-year-old Class 1 commercial pilot, tirzepatide was initiated during a non-flying period and was associated with early improvements in blood pressure, BMI, and glycemic parameters. At approximately four months, the pilot remained asymptomatic and reported no treatment-related adverse effects; ECG remained normal, and cardiology considered him clinically stable. These findings demonstrate a favorable clinical response to tirzepatide in the context of obesity and cardiometabolic risk, but do not establish fitness to fly.

The principal aeromedical consideration remained the cardiovascular presentation in February 2026, including accelerated hypertension and troponin elevation. The significance and underlying cause of the troponin elevation require assessment independently of the response to tirzepatide. Any consideration of return to flight should also address treatment stability, medication tolerability, hydration and nutritional status, potential performance-limiting adverse effects, concomitant therapies, and functional capacity. The responsible licensing or aeromedical authority makes the final determination of Class 1 fitness and should base it on applicable regulatory requirements and the evidence required for the individual case. Further clinical and aeromedical experience with GLP-1 and combined GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists in aircrew will be important in defining appropriate monitoring and certification requirements across different regulatory jurisdictions.

This case highlights the distinction between therapeutic response and aeromedical certification. While effective management of obesity and associated cardiometabolic risk may improve clinical status, return to commercial aviation requires an individualized, evidence-based, and jurisdiction-specific assessment of the underlying disease, treatment, functional status, and potential implications for operational safety.

abstract.heading: Background
abstract.text: Abdominal tuberculosis is an important form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis with a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations. Tuberculous peritonitis may present with nonspecific constitutional and systemic symptoms and minimal abdominal findings, making early diagnosis challenging. Negative microbiological testing of ascitic fluid does not necessarily exclude the disease. Tuberculous peritonitis may mimic other intra-abdominal infective or inflammatory conditions, and tissue diagnosis may be required when initial testing is inconclusive.

abstract.heading: Case presentation
abstract.text: A 16-year-old male school student presented with a 7-day history of high-grade intermittent fever associated with tiredness and body pain, along with occasional mild, vague abdominal discomfort. There was no history of vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria, or constipation, and no respiratory or urinary symptoms or relevant travel or exposure history. He had received cefoperazone-sulbactam and doxycycline at a local hospital without clinical improvement. On examination, he was febrile at 101°F with a few sub-centimetric cervical lymph nodes and minimal left iliac fossa tenderness. Initial investigations showed an elevated C-reactive protein level (CRP) of 195 mg/L, with otherwise preserved blood counts and organ function. Screening for common tropical infections was negative, and blood cultures showed no growth. Ultrasonography initially demonstrated minimal ascites. Subsequent CT abdomen and pelvis revealed moderate ascites, diffuse peritoneal thickening and enhancement, small peritoneal nodules, and diffuse omental thickening, raising suspicion of abdominal tuberculosis. Ascitic fluid cytology was negative for malignancy, and MTB/RIF Ultra did not detect *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*; however, the ascitic fluid adenosine deaminase level was markedly elevated (89.5 U/L). In view of persistent fever and characteristic radiologic findings, laparoscopic peritoneal and omental biopsy was performed. Tissue GeneXpert detected *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, while histopathology demonstrated well-formed granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes with Langhans-type and foreign-body-type giant cells and small foci of central necrosis, consistent with tuberculosis. Empirical anti-tubercular therapy was initiated after tissue sampling.

abstract.heading: Conclusion
abstract.text: This case highlights that abdominal tuberculosis should remain an important differential diagnosis in patients with persistent fever and nonspecific abdominal symptoms, even when initial screening for tuberculosis is negative and classical constitutional or pulmonary features are absent. Cross-sectional imaging, ascitic fluid ADA, and, most importantly, tissue sampling can establish the diagnosis in suspected tuberculous peritonitis.
