articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Abdominal tuberculosis is an important form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis and may involve the peritoneum, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, and solid abdominal organs. Its presentation is often nonspecific, with fever, abdominal discomfort, anorexia, constitutional symptoms, or ascites. Because these manifestations overlap with those of malignancy and other infectious or inflammatory disorders, diagnosis can be challenging. Imaging may reveal ascites, peritoneal thickening, nodularity, and omental involvement, but definitive diagnosis may require microbiological or histopathological confirmation. We report a case of tuberculous peritonitis with omental involvement in a 16-year-old boy who presented primarily with prolonged fever and only mild abdominal symptoms, with diagnosis established by laparoscopic biopsy.1,2

Case presentation

A 16-year-old male presented with a 7-day history of high-grade intermittent fever associated with generalized fatigue, body aches, and occasional vague abdominal discomfort. He had no gastrointestinal, respiratory, urinary, or joint symptoms and no significant travel or sick-contact history. He had received cefoperazone-sulbactam and doxycycline at a peripheral hospital from the second day of illness, but the fever persisted. On admission, he was febrile (101°F) with a few subcentimetric cervical lymph nodes and minimal left iliac fossa tenderness; the remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Investigations for common tropical infections, including dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, scrub typhus, and enteric fever, as well as Epstein-Barr virus infection, were negative. Blood cultures showed no growth. Ultrasonography initially demonstrated minimal ascites, while subsequent CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed moderate ascites with diffuse peritoneal thickening and enhancement, small peritoneal nodules, and diffuse omental thickening, raising suspicion of tuberculous peritonitis. Ascitic fluid showed lymphocyte-predominant inflammation with an elevated ADA of 89.5 U/L; however, MTB/RIF Ultra was negative, and cytology showed no malignant cells. In view of the persistent fever and characteristic radiological findings, diagnostic laparoscopic peritoneal and omental biopsy was performed. Tissue GeneXpert detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis, while histopathology showed well-formed, confluent necrotizing granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans-type giant cells; Ziehl-Neelsen and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains were negative. Based on the combined clinical, radiological, microbiological, and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of abdominal tuberculosis with tuberculous peritonitis and omental involvement was established. Anti-tubercular therapy was initiated following tissue sampling.

Discussion

This case illustrates the diagnostic challenge of abdominal tuberculosis when the presenting complaint is predominantly fever with only minimal abdominal symptoms. The patient had no respiratory symptoms, and his initial examination was relatively unremarkable apart from fever, a few cervical lymph nodes, and mild left iliac fossa tenderness. The inflammatory response was notable for a markedly elevated CRP despite a near-normal total leukocyte count.

The initial work-up for common tropical infections and other infectious causes was negative. Ultrasound initially showed only minimal ascites, whereas CT later demonstrated moderate ascites, diffuse peritoneal thickening and enhancement, peritoneal nodules, and diffuse omental thickening. These findings increased suspicion for peritoneal tuberculosis, but they can also occur in other inflammatory or malignant conditions. The negative ascitic MTB/RIF testing did not exclude the diagnosis. In this case, the elevated ascitic fluid ADA provided additional supportive evidence, while tissue sampling ultimately established the diagnosis.

The case also highlights the complementary role of microbiology and histopathology in extrapulmonary tuberculosis. GeneXpert detection of MTB in the biopsy sample provided microbiological confirmation, while histopathology demonstrated well-formed granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans-type giant cells, and small foci of necrosis. The negative Ziehl-Neelsen stain does not exclude tuberculosis, particularly in a paucibacillary extrapulmonary lesion when molecular and histopathological findings are concordant.

Early recognition of abdominal tuberculosis is important because delayed diagnosis may lead to progressive peritoneal disease and complications. A high index of suspicion, appropriate cross-sectional imaging, and timely tissue diagnosis are especially valuable when the clinical presentation is atypical and initial screening tests are nondiagnostic.1,2

Learning points

  • Abdominal tuberculosis should be considered in patients with prolonged or unexplained fever even when abdominal symptoms are mild and pulmonary symptoms are absent.
  • Peritoneal thickening, nodularity, ascites, and omental involvement on CT should raise suspicion of tuberculous peritonitis while also prompting consideration of other infective, inflammatory, and malignant causes.
  • A negative ascitic fluid Xpert MTB/RIF test does not exclude abdominal tuberculosis; ascitic fluid ADA and tissue diagnosis may be important in selected patients.
  • Laparoscopic peritoneal or omental biopsy can provide definitive microbiological and histopathological evidence when non-invasive investigations are inconclusive.
  • Concordant GeneXpert positivity and necrotizing granulomatous histopathology can establish the diagnosis even when Ziehl-Neelsen staining is negative.

Conclusion

This case highlights abdominal tuberculosis presenting predominantly as prolonged fever in a young patient with minimal abdominal symptoms and no respiratory manifestations. Initial screening for common tropical infections and ascitic MTB testing were negative, while CT imaging, elevated ascitic fluid ADA, and subsequent peritoneal/omental biopsy led to the diagnosis. Tissue GeneXpert detection and compatible necrotizing granulomatous histopathology confirmed tuberculous peritonitis with omental involvement. Maintaining a high index of suspicion and pursuing timely tissue diagnosis, when initial investigations are inconclusive, can facilitate early treatment in atypical presentations of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.

articles.title: Postpartum reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome presenting as progressive stroke without headache

affiliations.text: SRM Medical College Hospital & Research Centre, Chennai.

abstract.text: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is an under-recognized cause of postpartum stroke and is typically associated with thunderclap headache. We report a 35-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease who developed sudden-onset right hemiparesis on postpartum day 11, notably without headache. Serial magnetic resonance imaging over one week showed progressive bilateral infarcts in multiple territories. Angiography revealed diffuse, tapering arterial narrowing that initially involved the posterior circulation and later extended to the anterior circulation. Inflammatory markers and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal. She was treated with nimodipine, verapamil, hydration, and rehabilitation. Follow-up angiography at four months demonstrated complete restoration of vessel caliber with residual gliotic changes, confirming the diagnosis. Notably, postpartum RCVS may occur without headache, and demonstration of reversible cerebral arterial vasoconstriction remains a key diagnostic feature.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is characterized by multifocal narrowing of the cerebral arteries that usually resolves spontaneously within three months.1 Postpartum cerebral angiopathy, also known as Call-Fleming syndrome, refers to RCVS occurring during the puerperium and is an important cause of stroke in young women.2,5 Thunderclap headache is reported in 95-100% of patients and may be the only manifestation.3 We describe a woman with rheumatic heart disease in whom postpartum RCVS presented as a progressive hemispheric stroke without any headache.

Case report

A 35-year-old woman (P2L2) with a history of rheumatic heart disease delivered a healthy male baby by spontaneous vaginal delivery. The immediate postpartum period was uneventful. She subsequently underwent puerperal sterilisation, following which she developed chest pain. Electrocardiography, echocardiography, and computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography were normal except for moderate rheumatic mitral regurgitation. She was discharged on oral penicillin prophylaxis. There was no history of pre-eclampsia, seizures, headache, or use of vasoactive or recreational drugs.

Approximately a week later, she developed sudden-onset weakness of the right upper and lower limbs, with difficulty lifting her arm above shoulder level, holding a cup, wearing footwear, and climbing stairs. There was no headache, neck weakness, or bladder or bowel disturbance. Higher mental functions, speech, and cranial nerves were normal. Motor examination revealed right-sided hypotonia with grade 3/5 hemiparesis. Deep tendon reflexes were barely elicited, and hand grip strength was approximately 60%.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed hyperacute infarcts in the left frontal and left parieto-occipital regions. MR angiography (MRA) demonstrated diffuse narrowing of both vertebral arteries and the basilar artery. A postpartum cardioembolic stroke was the provisional diagnosis; anticoagulation was initiated, and Holter monitoring was planned.

Her weakness continued to progress, and repeat MRI showed enlargement of the left parieto-occipital infarct, with new infarcts in the right high frontal region, right centrum semiovale, and left corona radiata. MRA showed attenuation of the anterior cerebral and terminal middle cerebral arteries (Figure 1). CT cerebral angiography confirmed diffuse, smooth narrowing of both vertebral arteries, the basilar artery, and both posterior cerebral arteries. Hemoglobin and blood counts were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 22 mm in the first hour, and C-reactive protein was negative. Renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, lipid profile, and serum electrolytes were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was also unremarkable.

Over the subsequent week, she developed impaired comprehension and right-sided hemineglect, accompanied by further expansion of the cerebral infarcts and progression of the arterial attenuation. At this point, the differential diagnosis included primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS), posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), and RCVS. She was treated with nimodipine 60 mg every six hours and verapamil 120 mg once daily, along with adequate hydration, physiotherapy, and occupational therapy. Her neurological deficits stabilized and gradually improved. Follow-up MRI and MRA in December 2025 demonstrated complete restoration of the caliber of both the posterior and anterior circulation vessels, with residual gliosis in the previously infarcted territories (Figure 2).

Discussion

RCVS arises from a transient disturbance of the tone of the cerebral vessels, involving endothelial dysfunction, sympathetic overactivity, and disruption of the blood-brain barrier.1,2 The abrupt fall in estrogen levels following delivery may alter blood-brain barrier permeability and vascular reactivity. Other precipitants include serotonergic and sympathomimetic drugs, pre-eclampsia, and Valsalva-type manoeuvres.3,5

Two features of this case are noteworthy. First, headache was absent. Although thunderclap headache is the characteristic presenting symptom of RCVS, headache-free cases have been described and may be more frequently associated with neurological complications such as stroke.4,5 Therefore, the absence of headache does not exclude RCVS, particularly when angiography demonstrates diffuse, smooth, tapering arterial narrowing.

Second, both the neurological deficits and arterial abnormalities progressed for approximately one week after presentation. Vasoconstriction in RCVS typically peaks around two to three weeks after onset and spreads from distal to more proximal arteries.3 In our patient, the initial involvement of the posterior circulation was followed by involvement of the anterior circulation. Thus, early radiological progression of arterial narrowing and cerebral infarction does not necessarily indicate a wrong diagnosis or treatment failure.

Distinguishing RCVS from primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is important, since glucocorticoids have been associated with worse outcomes in RCVS.7 PACNS more commonly produces irregular, notched, eccentric stenoses with abnormal cerebrospinal fluid findings and insidious headache, whereas RCVS typically demonstrates smooth, tapering "string of beads" narrowing with normal cerebrospinal fluid.2 In our patient, normal inflammatory markers and cerebrospinal fluid findings, together with complete reversal of the angiographic abnormalities on follow-up, supported the diagnosis of RCVS. The RCVS2 score may also serve as a useful clinical adjunct in distinguishing RCVS from other cerebrovascular disorders.6 Treatment is primarily supportive, with calcium channel blockers and avoidance of triptans, ergots and intra-arterial vasodilators.1,4

Conclusion

RCVS should be considered in postpartum women presenting with acute focal neurological deficits and diffuse cerebral arterial narrowing, even in the absence of headache. Progressive neurological and angiographic abnormalities during the early phase should not by themselves exclude the diagnosis. Demonstration of reversible cerebral arterial narrowing on follow-up imaging, typically within 12 weeks, remains a key diagnostic feature of RCVS.

articles.title: Addressing the drivers of inappropriate antibiotic use in the outpatient setting

affiliations.text: Department of Infectious Diseases, KIMSHEALTH, Trivandrum, Kerala, India.

abstract.text: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, and inappropriate antibiotic use in outpatient settings is an important contributor. Although antimicrobial stewardship has traditionally focused on hospitalized patients, most antibiotics are prescribed in ambulatory care, where diagnostic uncertainty, fear of missing bacterial infection, action bias, patient expectations, knowledge gaps, self-medication, and health-system constraints can promote inappropriate prescribing. This review examines the major drivers of inappropriate outpatient antibiotic use and illustrates them through common clinical scenarios. It highlights practical approaches to stewardship, including diagnostic stewardship, guideline-based antibiotic selection, effective clinician-patient communication, delayed prescribing where appropriate, and audit and feedback. Particular attention is given to the WHO AWaRe framework and the challenges of implementing stewardship in resource-constrained settings such as India. Strengthening outpatient antimicrobial stewardship through behavioral, diagnostic, digital, regulatory, and health-system interventions is essential to improving antibiotic use and reducing the spread of AMR.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the greatest threats to global health, compromising the effective treatment of infectious diseases and increasing morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Antibiotic exposure remains the primary driver of resistance, making optimization of antibiotic use central to any strategy to combat AMR. While antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) have traditionally focused on hospitalized patients, increasing evidence suggests that outpatient settings represent an equally important battleground in the fight against AMR. The majority of antibiotics worldwide are prescribed in ambulatory care settings, including primary care clinics, emergency departments, urgent care centers, and specialty outpatient clinics. Importantly, a substantial proportion of these prescriptions are unnecessary or inappropriate. Studies from the United States estimate that approximately 30% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions may be inappropriate, highlighting significant opportunities for stewardship interventions.1

The challenge is particularly relevant in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as India, where outpatient departments often experience high patient volumes, limited consultation times, inadequate diagnostic infrastructure, and substantial pressure to prescribe medications. These factors contribute to widespread empirical antibiotic use and increase the risk of inappropriate prescribing. Evidence from public tertiary care hospitals in Bihar documented broad-spectrum antibiotic use in most outpatient encounters, culture testing in fewer than 3% of visits, and amoxicillin-clavulanate accounting for nearly 43% of all antibiotic prescriptions.2 India's National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR, 2017-2026) explicitly identifies outpatient stewardship as a priority intervention, yet implementation at the facility level remains inconsistent.

Unlike inpatient settings, outpatient antibiotic prescribing decisions are frequently made in the absence of microbiological confirmation and with limited opportunities for follow-up. Consequently, prescribing behavior is influenced not only by clinical considerations but also by psychological, social, organizational, and health-system factors. Understanding these drivers is essential for designing effective interventions that promote appropriate antibiotic use and reduce the burden of AMR.

The outpatient stewardship challenge

Outpatient settings account for the largest share of global antibiotic consumption. Common indications include respiratory tract infections (RTIs), urinary tract infections (UTIs), skin and soft tissue infections, dental infections, and gastrointestinal illnesses, many of which are self-limiting or viral. Prescribing antibiotics when they are not indicated, selecting unnecessarily broad-spectrum agents, or extending treatment durations beyond guideline recommendations all promote resistance at the individual and community levels. Beyond AMR, inappropriate use increases the risk of adverse drug reactions, Clostridioides difficile infection, microbiome disruption, and avoidable healthcare expenditure. Meaningful progress against AMR cannot be achieved without substantially improving prescribing practices in outpatient settings.

Drivers of inappropriate antibiotic use

1. Diagnostic uncertainty

Diagnostic uncertainty is one of the most common reasons for antibiotic prescribing in outpatient practice. Clinicians are often required to make treatment decisions based on symptoms and examination findings alone, without immediate access to diagnostic confirmation.

Clinical vignette 1 - Diagnostic uncertainty

A 24-year-old student presented with a two-day history of sore throat, low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and dry cough. Examination revealed mild pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudates or cervical lymphadenopathy. The Centor score was 1 (fever alone), placing the probability of Group A Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis below 10%. Despite this, the treating physician prescribed azithromycin, citing an inability to completely exclude bacterial infection.

This scenario is common. The Centor and McIsaac clinical prediction rules can reliably stratify GAS risk and reduce empiric prescribing, yet their application in practice is inconsistent. Rapid antigen detection tests (RADTs) for streptococcal infection, where available, allow confirmation or exclusion within minutes. Diagnostic stewardship, encompassing appropriate test selection and the use of validated clinical decision tools, should therefore be considered an integral component of any ASP. In resource-limited settings where RADTs are unavailable, clear guidance on watchful waiting with safety-net advice is a viable alternative.

2. Risk aversion and fear of missing infection

Many clinicians perceive the immediate consequences of undertreating a bacterial infection to be greater than the long-term consequences of antimicrobial resistance. This often results in "just-in-case" prescribing.

Clinical vignette 2 - Asymptomatic bacteriuria

A 72-year-old woman with diabetes attended a routine follow-up visit, reporting no urinary symptoms, fever, or flank pain. A urine culture sent as part of a health check-up grew Escherichia coli at >105 CFU/mL. The clinician prescribed a seven-day antibiotic course, concerned that untreated bacteriuria might progress to pyelonephritis or urosepsis.

The IDSA 2019 guidelines on asymptomatic bacteriuria (ABU) explicitly recommend against treatment in non-pregnant adults, including older patients and those with diabetes, outside of specific procedural indications.3 Treatment of ABU in these groups confers no benefit, exposes patients to adverse effects, and generates selective pressure for resistant organisms. Risk aversion is a cognitive bias amenable to targeted education; stewardship efforts should emphasize guideline adherence and encourage clinicians to distinguish between situations where treatment is beneficial and those where observation is appropriate.

3. Action bias and colonization vs. infection

Action bias describes the tendency to prefer intervention over observation, particularly when faced with uncertainty.

Clinical vignette 3 - Diabetic foot colonization

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attended a wound care clinic with a chronic, healing plantar ulcer. He was systemically well, with no fever, surrounding cellulitis, erythema or warmth, or signs consistent with osteomyelitis. A wound swab sent during routine review grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterococcus faecalis, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The clinician prescribed broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics despite the absence of any clinical signs of active infection.

This case highlights two stewardship principles. First, colonization should not be mistaken for infection. Chronic wounds are frequently colonized with bacteria, and positive cultures alone do not justify antibiotic therapy. Second, diagnostic tests should only be performed when the results are expected to influence management. Sending inappropriate cultures often creates pressure to act on microbiological findings that represent colonization rather than disease.

Diagnostic stewardship is therefore essential. Appropriate test selection is just as important as appropriate antibiotic selection. Unnecessary investigations frequently lead to unnecessary treatment.

4. Patient expectations and communication

Patient expectations are often perceived as a major driver of antibiotic prescribing. However, evidence suggests patients often seek reassurance and explanation rather than antibiotics.

Clinical vignette 4 - Infectious mononucleosis

A 27-year-old man presented with six days of fever, severe sore throat, fatigue, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Laboratory testing demonstrated lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes. The clinician diagnosed probable infectious mononucleosis and advised paracetamol for symptomatic relief, with no antibiotic prescribed. He left dissatisfied and sought a second opinion the following day. The second physician reached the same diagnosis but invested additional time explaining the viral etiology, the expected clinical course, and the rationale for withholding antibiotics. EBV serology was requested to confirm the diagnosis, and a review appointment was arranged for 72 hours later. Despite no change in management, the patient reported high satisfaction with the second consultation.

Note: Aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin) are contraindicated in EBV mononucleosis because they can cause a widespread drug-induced maculopapular exanthem in up to 80% of cases - an important prescribing hazard in this context.

Patient satisfaction often depends on communication rather than antibiotic prescribing. Effective counseling, reassurance, safety-net advice, and shared decision-making can reduce inappropriate antibiotic use while maintaining patient confidence. Where appropriate, the "delayed prescription" strategy (a prescription issued but advised to be filled only if symptoms fail to improve or worsen within 48-72 hours) is an evidence-based approach for acute RTIs that reduces antibiotic use while preserving patient confidence.4

5. Knowledge gaps and prescriber awareness

Inadequate familiarity with current guidelines, local resistance data, and the WHO AWaRe classification (Table 1) contributes to sub-optimal antibiotic selection.

Clinical vignette 5 - Uncomplicated UTI

A physician prescribed levofloxacin for acute uncomplicated cystitis in an otherwise healthy, non-pregnant woman aged 34, citing concern about treatment failure. Nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin - Access-group agents with well-established efficacy for uncomplicated lower UTI and considerably lower collateral resistance impact - were not considered. The clinician was unaware of IDSA or institutional treatment guidelines, or of local resistance data showing fluoroquinolone resistance among uropathogens exceeding 30%.

Unnecessary use of Watch-group fluoroquinolones when Access-group agents are appropriate represents a missed stewardship opportunity. The WHO AWaRe classification provides a practical, evidence-based framework for antibiotic selection and should be integrated into prescribing education and institutional guidelines. Where electronic medical records (EMRs) are available, AWaRe-based recommendations can be integrated into prescribing workflows, prioritizing Access antibiotics for common syndromes. EMRs may also incorporate default treatment durations for specific indications, requiring prescribers to provide justification when longer courses are selected. Regular audit against local antibiograms, paired with individual feedback, is among the most consistently effective outpatient stewardship interventions.6

6. Over-the-counter access and self-medication

In India and many other LMICs, antibiotics are still widely available without a prescription, despite regulations that restrict their sale. Under Schedule H1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, and carbapenems can only be dispensed with a prescription and require special record-keeping. However, enforcement of these regulations is often inconsistent, and dispensing antibiotics without a prescription remains common. Self-medication with antibiotics driven by prior experience, cost concerns, and low health literacy results in inappropriate agent selection, subtherapeutic dosing, and abbreviated treatment courses, all of which favor resistance selection. Community-based stewardship efforts and public awareness campaigns, including initiatives such as the World AMR Awareness Week, are therefore important alongside interventions aimed at improving prescribing practices within healthcare facilities.

7. Health-system barriers

Inappropriate antibiotic use is not solely the result of individual prescribing decisions. Healthcare systems themselves often create environments that encourage antibiotic overuse. High patient loads, short consultation times, and the absence of structured follow-up mechanisms make watchful waiting and detailed counseling difficult to operationalize.

Evidence from tertiary hospitals in Bihar illustrates the influence of health-system factors on prescribing behavior. Amoxicillin-clavulanate accounted for 42.8% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions, followed by azithromycin and cefixime.2 These antibiotics were also among the most consistently available medications within the centralized procurement system, suggesting that drug availability may influence prescribing patterns. The same study reported minimal culture use despite widespread antibiotic use, highlighting the challenges of high-volume outpatient practice.2

Addressing system-level barriers requires investment in diagnostic infrastructure, staffing, and digital health tools. Electronic medical records (EMRs) and computerized physician order entry systems can support appropriate prescribing by requiring documentation of the indication and intended duration of therapy, incorporating syndrome-specific treatment recommendations, and prioritizing Access-group antibiotics in accordance with stewardship principles. Default treatment durations for common infections can also be embedded within prescribing systems, with justification required for extended courses.

Regular audit and feedback have demonstrated sustained improvements in prescribing quality in outpatient settings.6 The CDC Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship (commitment, action, tracking and reporting, education, and expertise) provide a practical framework for program development.8

Future directions

Future outpatient stewardship efforts should integrate behavioral science, digital health technologies, and health-system reforms. Artificial intelligence-assisted decision-support tools, rapid point-of-care diagnostics, and automated prescribing dashboards may further improve antibiotic use. National AMR action plans should prioritize outpatient stewardship alongside hospital-based programs, particularly in countries such as India, where the majority of antibiotic consumption occurs in ambulatory care settings.

Clinical pearls

  • Outpatient settings account for the majority of global antibiotic use and are the primary drivers of community-level AMR.
  • Diagnostic uncertainty remains the most important driver of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing.
  • Clinical prediction scores (Centor/McIsaac) and rapid point-of-care tests should be used to stratify risk before prescribing for common syndromes such as pharyngitis and RTI.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated in non-pregnant adults, including older patients and those with diabetes (IDSA 2019).
  • Colonization should not be mistaken for infection; cultures from chronic wounds and indwelling devices should only be sent when the result will alter management.
  • Patient satisfaction is determined by communication quality, not antibiotic receipt. The delayed prescription strategy is a validated tool for acute RTIs.
  • Aminopenicillins are contraindicated in suspected EBV mononucleosis due to the risk of drug-induced exanthem.
  • The WHO AWaRe framework should guide first-line agent selection; Access antibiotics are appropriate for the majority of community-acquired infections.
  • OTC antibiotic availability and self-medication are major community-level resistance drivers that require regulatory enforcement alongside facility-based stewardship.
  • Audit and feedback is among the most effective outpatient stewardship interventions currently available.

articles.title: Managing obstructive sleep apnea: An evolving landscape of individualized treatment

affiliations.text: Department of Pulmonology and Sleep Medicine, Royal Bahrain Hospital, Sanad, Kingdom of Bahrain.

abstract.text: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common and frequently undertreated, not because effective therapies are lacking, but because matching treatment to the individual patient requires more than a reflexive prescription for continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). This review presents a concise clinical framework for OSA management: the pathophysiologic principles underlying treatment selection, CPAP as first-line therapy, and the expanding range of alternatives - oral appliances, positional therapy, surgery, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, and pharmacotherapy - that enable treatment to be tailored rather than applied uniformly. This review gives particular attention to two pharmacologic developments: tirzepatide, approved for OSA in adults with obesity, and AD109, an investigational agent that acts through a distinct neuromuscular mechanism and has shown promising phase 3 results.

Introduction

The clinical challenge in OSA is rarely the diagnosis itself; it is sustaining patients on effective therapy beyond the first few months. The scale of the problem remains considerable: an estimated 425 million adults aged 30-69 years have moderate-to-severe OSA worldwide, with nearly one billion affected once mild disease is included.1 OSA is linked to hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and increased mortality.1 Despite this, many affected individuals remain undiagnosed, and many of those diagnosed discontinue first-line therapy within a year. This review provides a practical framework covering the pathophysiology and diagnosis of OSA, with a primary focus on the management options available once OSA is confirmed.

Pathophysiology

The pharynx collapses during sleep when forces promoting airway closure - negative inspiratory pressure, soft-tissue weight, and peri-airway fat in obesity - exceed the dilating action of the genioglossus and other upper airway muscles. Although anatomical factors such as retrognathia, macroglossia, tonsillar hypertrophy, and a narrow oropharynx predispose to collapse, they do not fully explain OSA heterogeneity. Eckert and colleagues identified four non-anatomical "endotypic" traits that contribute to disease susceptibility and severity: a low arousal threshold, high loop gain (unstable ventilatory control), reduced pharyngeal dilator muscle responsiveness, and low waking lung volume.2

These traits have clinical relevance because their relative contribution varies between patients and may influence treatment response. A lean patient with high loop gain is unlikely to respond to an oral appliance the way an anatomically obstructed patient would, which explains why newer pharmacologic agents (see Pharmacotherapy) target the neuromuscular component directly. Repeated apneas and hypopneas produce cycles of hypoxemia-reoxygenation and arousal, driving sympathetic activation, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction - the substrate linking OSA to cardiometabolic disease.1,2 Figure 1 summarizes this sequence.

Diagnosis

Classic symptoms - snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness - remain common, but many patients, particularly women and older adults, present atypically with fatigue, morning headache, or mood change. STOP-BANG and the Berlin Questionnaire can help identify patients at increased risk before objective testing.3 Diagnosis requires objective sleep testing: in-laboratory polysomnography remains the reference standard, particularly for patients with significant comorbidities or an inconclusive home sleep apnea test, whereas home sleep apnea testing is appropriate for adults with a high pretest probability of moderate to severe OSA and no major comorbidity.3 Severity is graded by the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI): mild 5-14.9 events/hour, moderate 15-29.9 events/hour, severe ≥30 events/hour. AHI should be interpreted alongside symptom burden, comorbidities, and other clinical factors rather than in isolation.3

Principles of treatment selection

Management should be individualized: address modifiable risk factors, including weight, sleep position, alcohol, sedatives, and smoking; select a primary airway therapy based on disease severity, anatomy, and likely adherence; treat accompanying comorbidities; and establish structured follow-up to assess both disease control and continued treatment use.

Positive airway pressure therapy

CPAP remains first-line therapy for most patients with moderate-to-severe OSA, pneumatically splinting the airway open.4 Evidence consistently demonstrates improvements in sleepiness, quality of life, and blood pressure, whereas evidence for reduction in major cardiovascular outcomes is less consistent.4 The inconsistent evidence for cardiovascular outcomes may in part reflect limited adherence in clinical trials. Auto-titrating PAP, which can be initiated at home, is now a practical default; bilevel PAP is generally reserved for patients intolerant of high fixed pressure or who have coexisting hypoventilation.

Adherence, rather than the device itself, most often determines treatment success. Common barriers include mask discomfort, nasal congestion, claustrophobia, and partner-related concerns. The formal adherence threshold (≥4 hours/night on ≥70% of nights) is a pragmatic regulatory benchmark; incremental use continues to confer benefit up to full-night coverage.4 Early follow-up within one to two weeks, heated humidification, alternative mask interfaces, structured education, and device download data can all help improve adherence in practice.

Oral appliance therapy

Mandibular advancement devices reposition the mandible and tongue base anteriorly, enlarging the retroglossal airway. They are recommended as a first-line option for selected patients with mild-to-moderate OSA who prefer an oral appliance to PAP, and as an alternative for patients who are intolerant of or unable to adhere to PAP.5 CPAP produces a greater reduction in AHI on a population basis, but higher adherence with oral appliances can narrow the difference in effectiveness in routine practice. Devices should be custom-fitted by a dentist trained in dental sleep medicine, with follow-up studies to confirm AHI control, rather than relying on symptoms alone.5

Positional therapy and weight management

Patients with strongly position-dependent AHI can benefit from vibrotactile positional trainers that discourage supine sleep, although adherence data remain more limited than for PAP. Weight loss of even 5-10% can measurably reduce AHI, while greater weight loss through lifestyle change, pharmacotherapy, or bariatric surgery can lead to remission in some patients.6 However, OSA may persist despite weight loss, particularly when longstanding obesity has contributed to persistent upper airway anatomical or physiological abnormalities.

Pharmacotherapy

Tirzepatide

Tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, was approved by the FDA in December 2024 for treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity, in conjunction with diet and increased physical activity.7 In the SURMOUNT-OSA program, tirzepatide produced a substantial reduction in AHI at 52 weeks compared with placebo in both patients unable or unwilling to use PAP and those using PAP.7 This is considerably larger than expected from weight loss alone. Tirzepatide therefore represents an important addition (with trial-level evidence) to the treatment landscape for patients with OSA and obesity, particularly those who are unable or unwilling to use PAP.7 Caveats remain - and include gradual dose escalation to improve gastrointestinal tolerability, cost and access barriers, and the lack of long-term data on the trajectory of OSA after treatment discontinuation. Figure 2 outlines how weight loss with tirzepatide may translate into improvements in upper airway function.

AD109 (Aroxybutynin/Atomoxetine)

AD109 is not yet an approved therapy; it is discussed here because the phase 3 data are now published and clinically relevant. It is a once-daily combination of an antimuscarinic (aroxybutynin) and a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (atomoxetine), designed to preserve genioglossus and dilator muscle activity during sleep independent of body weight (Figure 3). In the SynAIRgy and LunAIRo phase 3 trials, which enrolled adults with mild-to-severe OSA who were unable or unwilling to use PAP, AD109 produced a placebo-adjusted AHI reduction of approximately 4 events/hour over 26 weeks, with improvements in oxygen desaturation index and fatigue.8 This is more modest than typically seen with CPAP or tirzepatide. Still, a significantly greater proportion of participants receiving AD109 achieved a ≥50% reduction in AHI compared with placebo, with no excess of serious adverse events, and the treatment effect was observed across patients irrespective of body weight.8 These findings suggest a potential role for AD109 in patients who cannot tolerate or decline PAP, with few effective alternatives.9,10 At the time of writing, AD109 has not been approved by the FDA, the European Medicines Agency, or other regulatory authorities, and this review should not be read as recommending its use outside a clinical trial setting.

Surgical management

Surgery is generally considered for patients with anatomically correctable obstruction or for those unable to use PAP or an oral appliance. Options include uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy (effective where tonsillar hypertrophy is a major contributor, and first-line surgery in children), maxillomandibular advancement (which can provide among the most durable results, particularly in younger patients), and nasal surgery, which rarely resolves OSA on its own but may improve CPAP tolerance. Drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) has become routine for surgical planning, visualizing the site and pattern of collapse under sedation. In patients with severe obesity, bariatric surgery can produce substantial weight loss and meaningful, though often incomplete, AHI improvement. PAP should generally be continued during the interim.6

Hypoglossal nerve stimulation

Hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HGNS) is an established option for selected patients with moderate-to-severe OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP.11 An implanted system senses the respiratory cycle and stimulates the hypoglossal nerve, producing anterior tongue displacement during inspiration. Candidacy requires a DISE excluding complete concentric palatal collapse, BMI below a defined threshold, and AHI in the moderate-to-severe range without a substantial central component; adherence generally exceeds that seen with PAP, given the absence of a nightly mask interface.11 HGNS is not currently available, for example, in Bahrain or elsewhere in the region; suitable candidates may therefore require referral abroad where feasible. It is presented here as a potential option for carefully selected, treatment-exhausted patients rather than a locally accessible pathway.

Special populations

OSA treatment forms part of the broader management strategy in patients with resistant hypertension and in selected patients with recurrent atrial fibrillation after ablation. However, evidence that PAP reduces major cardiovascular outcomes remains inconsistent.4 Expectations should therefore be discussed in terms of established benefits, rather than presumed cardiovascular protection. Undiagnosed OSA carries real perioperative risk, warranting proactive screening before major surgery. When obesity hypoventilation coexists with OSA, bilevel PAP should replace CPAP alone, alongside aggressive weight management.4

Long-term follow-up

OSA requires the same longitudinal attention as other chronic diseases, with reassessment of symptoms, treatment adherence, weight, and blood pressure at follow-up visits. Device downloads and telemonitoring can help identify and correct mask leaks or declining use early. Substantial changes in weight or anatomy should prompt reassessment of the original prescription.

Conclusion

OSA management has moved well beyond a single default prescription of CPAP. CPAP remains the first-line and best-studied therapy for moderate-to-severe disease. Still, oral appliances, positional therapy, surgery, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, and pharmacotherapy each have a role depending on the patient's phenotype, anatomy, and preferences. Tirzepatide has expanded the therapeutic options for adults with obesity and OSA who are unable or unwilling to use PAP.7 At the same time, AD109, if its phase 3 findings translate into regulatory approval and broader clinical evidence, could provide a mechanism-based option for patients who cannot use PAP, including those without obesity.8–10 None of these developments replace careful phenotyping and an honest discussion with patients about what they are realistically prepared and able to use consistently every night.

These technologies may enable earlier detection, improved risk stratification, individualized care, and greater access to specialist expertise. The future of pediatric cardiology is likely to be increasingly connected, personalized, and predictive, with technology complementing clinical expertise.

Introduction

Pediatric cardiology is undergoing a remarkable transformation. Advances in fetal diagnosis, neonatal intensive care, cardiac surgery, and catheter-based interventions have dramatically improved survival of children with congenital and acquired heart disease. The specialty is now moving beyond conventional diagnosis and treatment toward artificial intelligence (AI), digital health, remote monitoring, precision medicine, advanced imaging, and minimally invasive interventions.

The pediatric cardiologist of the future may work not only with echocardiographic images and catheter-based procedures, but also with AI-driven risk predictions, remotely collected physiological data, and wearable biosensors capable of detecting deterioration before a child becomes critically ill.

New guidelines, changing landscape

One of the most important recent developments is the 2025 International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) Guideline for the Management of Pediatric Heart Failure, the first major update to the 2014 guidance. The guideline incorporates advances in the pharmacological treatment, evaluation, and management of children with heart failure, while emphasizing the distinctive nature of pediatric disease.

Pediatric heart failure is not simply a smaller version of adult heart failure. Children may develop heart failure because of cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, acquired myocardial disease, or complex postoperative physiology. Contemporary care increasingly incorporates biomarkers, advanced echocardiography including strain imaging, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, optimization of medical therapy, early recognition of advanced heart failure, mechanical circulatory support, and transplantation.1

AI in pediatric cardiology

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly emerging as an important complementary tool in pediatric cardiology. Machine learning and deep learning can analyze complex and heterogeneous data and support diagnosis, risk stratification, imaging interpretation, and clinical decision-making.2

AI's greatest potential may lie not in replacing the pediatric cardiologist, but in augmenting clinical reasoning and improving efficiency. Current applications span electrocardiography, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, congenital heart disease imaging, and procedural planning.3

AI and the ECG

The electrocardiogram may evolve from a conventional tool for assessing rhythm and conduction into a richer source of diagnostic and prognostic information. AI-enabled ECG analysis is being explored for the detection of arrhythmias, ventricular dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, channelopathies, and congenital heart disease.4

Of particular interest is AI's potential to identify subtle electrical patterns that may not be readily apparent on conventional visual interpretation.

However, widespread implementation requires rigorous pediatric validation. Age-dependent ECG patterns, relatively small pediatric datasets, and the anatomical heterogeneity of congenital heart disease present unique challenges for the development and generalizability of AI models.4

AI in echocardiography and cardiac imaging

Echocardiography remains the cornerstone of pediatric cardiology but is highly dependent on operator skill and experience. AI can assist with image acquisition, view classification, image quality assessment, image segmentation, automated measurements, and detection of congenital heart disease patterns.5

AI may also improve standardization and reproducibility in cardiac MRI and CT analysis. In remote or resource-limited settings, AI-guided image acquisition combined with telecardiology could expand access to specialist expertise. However, robust validation and integration into clinical workflows will be essential before such approaches can be widely adopted.5

Wearable biosensors and remote monitoring

Wearable biosensors enable continual, noninvasive monitoring of physiological and behavioral parameters in patients with pediatric or congenital heart disease. Devices using photoplethysmography, ECG, and accelerometry can potentially monitor heart rate, rhythm, oxygen saturation, and physical activity.

Potential applications include smartwatches, ECG patches, activity monitors, and smartphone-linked physiological sensors. These technologies may be particularly relevant to cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, Fontan circulation, single ventricle physiology, repaired Tetralogy of Fallot, and pediatric heart failure. However, important challenges remain, including hardware design, data accuracy, integration into clinical workflows, privacy, and the need for pediatric-specific validation.6

Remote monitoring of pediatric heart failure

One of the potentially important applications of digital health is the remote monitoring of children with heart failure. Parameters that may be collected include heart rate, rhythm, activity, sleep, respiratory patterns, oxygen saturation, and body weight. The clinical value of such monitoring may lie less in individual measurements than in longitudinal trends.

For example, a sustained reduction in physical activity accompanied by a rising resting heart rate, increasing respiratory rate, or weight gain could potentially signal early clinical deterioration. AI-based systems may eventually integrate these data and generate risk alerts for the pediatric cardiology team to review. At present, this remains an evolving field and should complement - not replace - clinical assessment and established pediatric heart failure management pathways.7

Home monitoring in congenital heart disease

Home monitoring is already an established component of care in selected high-risk congenital heart disease populations. The American Heart Association scientific statement on interstage home monitoring highlights surveillance strategies for infants with shunt-dependent single ventricle heart disease and emphasizes the importance of early detection of physiologic changes that may precede decompensation.7

Digital platforms, telehealth, and automated alerts may further strengthen these monitoring programs. Remote monitoring can therefore serve as a model for future care of other medically complex pediatric cardiac populations.

Implantable and chest-based monitoring

In adult cardiovascular medicine, implanted and device-based systems can provide information on rhythm, activity, respiratory patterns, and selected hemodynamic surrogates. Translation of these technologies to children is promising but remains constrained by body size, growth, complex congenital anatomy, device availability, and limited pediatric evidence.

Future pediatric-specific sensors may allow increasingly continuous monitoring. However, such technologies require careful validation in children, and their potential applications should be distinguished from established standards of care.8

3D printing, virtual reality and simulation

Patient-specific 3D models are increasingly used to improve understanding of complex congenital anatomy. In pediatric congenital heart disease, 3D printing has applications in education, communication, preoperative planning, simulation, and selected surgical or interventional procedures.9

Future applications may increasingly combine CT or MRI data with 3D reconstruction, virtual or mixed reality, and procedure-specific simulations. These technologies may be particularly valuable in patients with complex ventricular relationships, great artery anatomy, pulmonary arteries, aortic arch abnormalities, and complex intracardiac defects.

The changing face of pediatric interventional cardiology

Interventional pediatric cardiology continues to evolve toward lower-profile devices, neonatal interventions, hybrid procedures, and advanced imaging guidance. Greater emphasis is being placed on precise procedural planning and reducing radiation and contrast exposure.

Future catheterization laboratories may increasingly integrate echocardiography, fluoroscopy, CT, MRI, and 3D reconstruction. These advances are particularly relevant in children because of their greater sensitivity to ionizing radiation and longer expected lifetime after exposure. AI-based tools and patient-specific computational modeling may further support procedural planning and risk assessment.

Precision medicine and genetics

The movement towards personalized cardiovascular care is another important trend in pediatric cardiology. Similar clinical phenotypes may have different genetic, metabolic, or acquired causes and may therefore require different approaches to surveillance and treatment.

The future model may integrate clinical phenotype, genetics, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and AI-based risk prediction. AI is increasingly being explored as a tool to integrate these complex and heterogeneous datasets, although explainability, generalizability, and equity remain important concerns.

Tele-pediatric cardiology

Digital technology may be particularly important in regions with limited access to pediatric cardiologists. A future care pathway could connect a primary healthcare center with digital ECG acquisition, AI-supported analysis, echocardiography, secure image transfer, and remote pediatric cardiology review.

Tele-pediatric cardiology may support screening, echocardiography review, postoperative follow-up, heart failure surveillance, and arrhythmia care. AI should be viewed as a tool to extend specialist expertise rather than replace clinical judgment.

The future

Predictive rather than reactive cardiology

Traditional care is often reactive: the child becomes unwell → presents to hospital → diagnosis → treatment.

The emerging model is different: continuous monitoring → detection of abnormal trends → risk prediction → early intervention → prevention of deterioration.

This transition toward more predictive and preventive pediatric cardiology is one of the most important potential benefits of digital health. However, technology must complement clinical judgment. Children have unique physiology and rapidly changing developmental needs, and technologies developed for adults cannot simply be transferred to pediatric practice without validation.

Conclusion

Pediatric cardiology is entering a new era. AI, wearable biosensors, remote monitoring, advanced imaging, 3D modeling, precision medicine, and minimally invasive interventions are increasingly shaping the diagnosis and management of children with heart disease.

AI-enabled ECG analysis may improve diagnostic detection and risk stratification. AI-assisted echocardiography may support image acquisition and standardization. Wearable technologies and remote monitoring may allow earlier recognition of physiological deterioration. Meanwhile, interventional cardiology continues to advance through smaller devices, hybrid approaches, and increasingly sophisticated imaging.

The future of pediatric cardiology is likely to be more connected, more personalized, and more predictive. Yet technology will remain a means rather than an end. The pediatric cardiologist will continue to play the central role in interpreting complex data, integrating it with clinical context, and making decisions that recognize not only the disease but also the child behind the data.

abstract.text: India's medico-legal environment is undergoing significant transformation. The implementation of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), increasing digitization of medical records, evolving jurisprudence on end-of-life care, and emerging concerns about artificial intelligence in healthcare have collectively redefined the legal responsibilities of healthcare institutions and practitioners. These developments extend beyond legal theory and directly affect clinical practice, documentation standards, informed consent processes, and hospital governance. This article reviews key recent medico-legal developments in India and highlights their practical implications for healthcare professionals. Understanding these evolving medico-legal expectations is essential to strengthen patient safety and clinical governance and minimize legal risk in current healthcare practice.

articles.bodyHtml:
Introduction

Medicine has always functioned at the intersection of science, ethics, and law. In recent years, rapid technological advancement, increased patient awareness, greater judicial scrutiny, and legislative reforms have substantially transformed India's medico-legal landscape.5,6 Hospitals are no longer judged solely by clinical outcomes. Increasingly, documentation quality, communication, transparency, and regulatory compliance influence both professional accountability and legal outcomes.5,7 For healthcare professionals, understanding these developments is no longer optional. Awareness of evolving legal expectations has become an essential component of safe clinical practice and effective risk management.7,14

The new criminal laws and their relevance to healthcare

One of the most significant legal reforms in independent India has been the replacement of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), and Indian Evidence Act with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA).1,3

These laws have important implications for medical practice. The new framework places greater emphasis on electronic evidence, digital documentation, and procedural safeguards in cases involving allegations of medical negligence.1,3

Electronic medical records, digital consent forms, audit trails, and time-stamped clinical notes have assumed increasing importance in legal proceedings. For hospitals, this underscores the need for robust electronic record systems, secure data storage, and standardized documentation practices.14

Digital transformation of medico-legal practice

The transition from paper-based records to digital platforms represents one of the most important medico-legal developments of recent years. Several states have implemented digital medico-legal reporting systems that enable standardized, digitally signed medico-legal reports and postmortem documentation.4,8

These systems improve transparency, accountability, traceability, and accessibility while reducing the risks associated with illegible handwriting and document tampering. Digital documentation also facilitates integration with law enforcement and judicial systems, enabling more efficient investigations and better coordination among stakeholders.4

Documentation: The strongest medico-legal defense

Despite advances in medicine, the fundamental medico-legal principle remains unchanged: good documentation is often the strongest defense against allegations of negligence.10,20

Courts frequently evaluate not only the clinical decision itself but also the quality of documentation supporting that decision. In many cases, inadequate or absent documentation can weaken the clinician's ability to demonstrate that appropriate care was provided. Conversely, well-maintained records can provide important evidence of sound clinical judgment.10

Comprehensive documentation should include clinical findings, differential diagnoses, treatment rationale, informed consent discussions, communication with patients and relatives, and details of follow-up advice.7,14,20

Informed consent: Beyond a signature

The concept of informed consent has evolved considerably. Contemporary legal standards require viewing consent as a process rather than a formality.9

Patients are increasingly expected to receive information regarding diagnosis, proposed treatment, alternatives, potential complications, anticipated outcomes, and limitations of care before making decisions.9,14

Generic consent forms, incomplete documentation of counseling, and language barriers continue to be major causes of medico-legal disputes. Hospitals should therefore ensure that consent procedures are procedure-specific, understandable to the patient, and appropriately documented.9

End-of-life care and the right to die with dignity

Recent judicial developments have reinforced the constitutional principle that dignity extends to the end of life. Courts have emphasized the role of medical boards, surrogate decision-making, advance directives, and palliative care in end-of-life situations.12,13

These developments have important implications for intensive care units and tertiary care hospitals. Institutions should periodically review their policies regarding end-of-life care, Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) orders, advance directives, and multidisciplinary decision-making.2,3

Medical records as a patient right

Recent judicial observations have strengthened the principle that access to medical records is a fundamental patient right.5,15 Hospitals are increasingly expected to provide medical records promptly and transparently.

Delays in providing records may be viewed as a service deficiency and may adversely affect an institution's position in litigation. Healthcare organizations should establish standardized procedures for the timely release of medical records while ensuring confidentiality and privacy.4,15

Artificial intelligence: The next medico-legal frontier

Artificial intelligence is rapidly entering clinical practice through diagnostic support systems, predictive analytics, imaging interpretation, robotic surgery, and administrative automation.

While AI offers substantial opportunities, it also raises complex medico-legal questions concerning accountability, liability, transparency, and patient safety. Current legal thinking suggests that responsibility for clinical decisions ultimately remains with the treating physician, even when those decisions are informed by AI-generated recommendations.17

Healthcare institutions should therefore establish governance frameworks addressing the validation and safe deployment of AI systems, physician oversight, documentation of AI-assisted decisions, and risk management.17

Practical recommendations for healthcare institutions

The evolving medico-legal landscape requires healthcare institutions to adopt a proactive approach that integrates legal compliance with quality patient care. The following strategic priorities can help strengthen medico-legal preparedness:

  1. Strengthen documentation systems: Standardized documentation practices supported by robust Electronic Medical Record (EMR) systems, regular documentation audits, and secure preservation of electronic records are essential for ensuring continuity of care and legal defensibility.4
  2. Standardize informed consent: Incorporate procedure-specific consent forms, effective patient counseling, and clear documentation of risks, benefits, alternatives, and patient understanding into routine clinical practice to minimize consent-related disputes.7
  3. Promote medico-legal education: Incorporate regular training programs for clinicians and healthcare staff on documentation standards, communication skills, medico-legal case management, telemedicine, and recent legal developments into continuing medical education.8
  4. Strengthen clinical governance: Hospitals should establish multidisciplinary governance mechanisms involving clinicians, administrators, quality teams, and legal experts to periodically review medico-legal cases, adverse events, patient complaints, and documentation practices, thereby promoting continuous quality improvement.14
  5. Prepare for digital healthcare: With increasing adoption of artificial intelligence, telemedicine, and digital health technologies, institutions should develop governance frameworks that address data privacy, cybersecurity, AI-assisted decision-making, and physician oversight to ensure safe, ethical, and legally compliant healthcare delivery.17

Ultimately, medico-legal resilience depends on a culture of quality, transparency, ethical practice, effective communication, and meticulous documentation. Healthcare organizations that proactively embrace these principles will be better equipped to deliver safe, patient-centered, and legally defensible care.

Conclusion

The medico-legal environment in India is evolving rapidly. The shift toward digital evidence, enhanced documentation standards, patient-centric consent processes, and emerging technologies is reshaping the legal expectations placed on healthcare providers. Although these developments may present new challenges, they also offer opportunities to strengthen patient trust, improve care quality, and reduce medico-legal risk. Ultimately, medico-legal safety will depend not only on clinical competence but also on integrating sound medical judgment, ethical practice, effective communication, and meticulous documentation.

In modern healthcare, excellence in documentation, communication, and professionalism is no longer merely desirable; it is an essential component of safe and legally defensible patient care. Healthcare organizations that integrate clinical excellence with ethical practice, digital governance, robust documentation, and medico-legal preparedness will be better positioned to navigate the evolving legal landscape while maintaining high standards of patient care.

pharma.summary: Three landmark studies presented in June 2026 suggest the kidney and cardiovascular benefits of finerenone may extend to non-diabetic CKD and glomerular diseases.

pharma.bodyHtml:
Finerenone is a selective, non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) initially approved for patients with chronic kidney disease associated with type 2 diabetes. It reduces the risk of kidney disease progression and cardiovascular complications in this population.

More recently, growing evidence from major studies has suggested that the potential benefits of finerenone may extend beyond diabetic kidney disease to non-diabetic CKD and certain glomerular diseases.

The findings were presented in June 2026 at the European Renal Association Congress in Glasgow, UK, and were reported in three major medical journals: The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA, and The Lancet.

1. Finerenone in patients with chronic kidney disease due to glomerular diseases

The study, 'Finerenone in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease Due to Glomerular Diseases: A Randomized Clinical Trial,' published in JAMA on June 5, 2026, evaluated the efficacy and safety of finerenone in patients with CKD due to glomerular diseases. The analysis was based on patients with glomerular diseases enrolled in the FIND-CKD trial.

The study found that treatment with finerenone was associated with a slower decline in kidney function, reduced albuminuria, and a lower risk of kidney failure or a sustained substantial decline in kidney function. These findings suggest that finerenone may have a role in preserving kidney function in selected patients with glomerular diseases.

2. Finerenone in persons with chronic kidney disease without diabetes

Finerenone in Persons with Chronic Kidney Disease without Diabetes (FIND-CKD), a large phase III trial in patients with non-diabetic CKD, was published in The New England Journal of Medicine on June 4, 2026. The study evaluated whether finerenone could provide kidney and cardiovascular benefits in patients with non-diabetic CKD similar to those previously observed in patients with diabetic CKD.

The study found that, among adults with CKD without diabetes, finerenone treatment resulted in a slower decline in eGFR than placebo over 32 months. Finerenone also reduced the risk of the composite kidney or cardiovascular outcome. These findings suggest that finerenone may help preserve kidney function in selected patients with non-diabetic CKD.

3. Finerenone across diabetic and non-diabetic CKD

In an analysis led by A/Prof Neuen and published in The Lancet, researchers pooled data from FIND-CKD with two previous phase III trials of finerenone in diabetic CKD. The analysis included 14,574 patients with diabetic and non-diabetic CKD.

Finerenone reduced the risk of CKD progression by 24% compared with placebo and reduced the risk of hospitalization for heart failure or cardiovascular death by 20%. The risk of all-cause death was also reduced by 12%. The effects were broadly consistent across diabetes status and different characteristics of kidney disease.

Together, these studies provide encouraging evidence that finerenone's benefits may extend beyond patients with diabetic kidney disease. They also provide a rationale for further evaluation of finerenone in non-diabetic CKD and glomerular diseases.

Further evidence and regulatory decisions will determine the extent to which these findings translate into routine clinical practice.

pharma.title: Aspirin: facts and insights
pharma.summary: Why aspirin comes in 81 mg and 325 mg strengths, and why 75 mg, 81 mg and 100 mg doses give similar antiplatelet effects.
pharma.bodyHtml:
Why is aspirin available in 81 mg and 325 mg doses?

Have you ever wondered why aspirin is commonly available in 81 mg and 325 mg doses rather than 80 mg or 300 mg?

The answer is partly rooted in the history of pharmaceutical measurement.

Before the widespread adoption of the metric system, physicians and pharmacists in Europe commonly used the apothecaries' system of weights and measures when prescribing and compounding medicines. This system included units such as the grain, scruple, dram (drachm), ounce, and pound.

The grain was particularly important because it provided a small unit suitable for measuring medicinal substances. Historically, medications such as aspirin, codeine, and morphine were often prescribed in grains rather than milligrams.

A standard adult dose of aspirin was historically 5 grains, which is approximately equivalent to 325 mg. A commonly used low-dose strength of 1¼ grains converts to approximately 81 mg.

Although the apothecaries' system is no longer used as the standard system for prescribing medications, its historical influence remains evident in modern pharmaceutical dosing.

Thus, the 81 mg dose is not simply an arbitrary choice between 80 and 85 mg. It is, in part, a legacy of the historical transition from the apothecaries' system to the metric system.

Is there any difference between aspirin 75 mg, 81 mg, and 100 mg?

The 75 mg, 81 mg and 100 mg doses of aspirin are all considered low-dose (or 'baby') aspirin and are commonly used for long-term antiplatelet therapy. There is generally little difference in their antiplatelet effect when used as maintenance therapy, although the appropriate dose depends on the clinical indication and relevant guidelines.

The variation in strengths largely reflects regional and historical differences in pharmaceutical formulations: 81 mg is commonly used in the United States, whereas 75 mg and 100 mg are common strengths in the UK, Europe and many other countries.

Why can 75 mg, 81 mg and 100 mg of aspirin provide similar antiplatelet effects?

The cumulative nature of aspirin's antiplatelet effect helps explain why different low-dose strengths - such as 75 mg, 81 mg and 100 mg once daily - can provide similar antiplatelet effects.

Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), thereby suppressing the production of thromboxane A2 (TXA2) and reducing platelet aggregation. Because this inhibition is irreversible, the effect persists for the lifespan of the affected platelet. Repeated daily doses therefore maintain inhibition as new platelets enter the circulation.

Once substantial platelet COX-1 inhibition has been achieved, increasing the dose within the low-dose range does not necessarily produce a proportionally greater antiplatelet effect. Thus, 75 mg, 81 mg, and 100 mg daily can all provide effective inhibition of platelet TXA2 production in many patients.

However, this does not mean that these doses are interchangeable for every clinical situation. Treatment decisions should always be guided by the relevant clinical guidelines and the individual patient's clinical condition and risk factors.

pharma.title: ISMP targeted medication safety best practices: Part III
pharma.summary: Selected ISMP Targeted Medication Safety Best Practices for Hospitals (2026-2027): opioid status, medication reconciliation, vaccine safety, IV push medications and barcode scanning.
refs: Institute for Safe Medication Practices. ISMP Targeted Medication Safety Best Practices for Hospitals, 2026-2027. https://online.ecri.org/hubfs/ISMP/Resources/ISMP_TargetedMedicationSafetyBestPractices_Hospitals.pdf
pharma.bodyHtml:
To reduce the risk of medication errors, the Institute for Safe Medication Practices (ISMP) developed the Targeted Medication Safety Best Practices for Hospitals to identify, inspire, and mobilize widespread adoption of consensus-based strategies addressing specific medication-safety issues that continue to cause fatal and harmful errors in patients.

In this series, we continue with a selection of Best Practices. Earlier selections were covered in previous issues.

Best Practice 15

Verify and document a patient's opioid status (naïve versus tolerant) and type of pain (acute versus chronic) before prescribing and dispensing extended-release and long-acting opioids.

Rationale: The goals of this Best Practice are:

  1. To support appropriate prescribing of extended-release and long-acting opioid medications and prevent death and serious patient harm from inappropriate use of these medications.
  2. To specifically prevent the inappropriate use of fentaNYL patches to treat acute pain in opioid-naïve patients.

Best Practice 21

Establish organizational expectations for complete medication reconciliation at admission, at all changes in the level of care, including transitions to and from the perioperative setting, and at discharge.

Rationale: The goal of this Best Practice is to eliminate medication errors during transitions in patient care.

Drug omissions, wrong doses, wrong drugs, additional drugs, and drugs inappropriate for the patient's current level of care or care setting have all resulted from errors during transitions in the continuum of patient care.

Best Practice 22

Safeguard against errors with vaccines administered in the inpatient and associated outpatient settings.

  • a. Utilize standard order sets to prescribe vaccines, require an order before administration, use the full generic name and brand name when applicable, and avoid vaccine abbreviations.
  • b. Verify a patient's immunization status in the electronic health record (EHR) and vaccine registries before providing vaccines.
  • c. Provide patients and/or caregivers with vaccine information, such as the Vaccine Information Statement (VIS), in their primary language before vaccination.
  • d. Store vaccines in separate bins or containers based on type and formulation. Store two-component vaccines together.
  • e. Use prefilled syringes when available. If they are not available, prepare each vaccine dose immediately before administration and label it appropriately.

Rationale: Errors with vaccines can result in unintended and unrecognized vulnerability, leaving patients unprotected against serious diseases.

New Best Practice 23 (2026-2027)

Improve safety with the use of intravenous (IV) push medications.

  • a. Optimize the use of ready-to-administer (RTA) medications.
  • b. Minimize unnecessary dilution and reconstitution of IV push medications outside a pharmacy. Eliminate the practice of diluting medications in sodium chloride flush syringes.
  • c. If the rate of an IV push medication is not practical to administer manually (e.g., over 5 minutes), use an infusion pump with dose error-reduction systems (DERS).

Rationale: The administration of IV push medications presents persistent safety risks. Use of RTA medications significantly reduces opportunities for error by eliminating unnecessary manipulation, reducing contamination risks, and ensuring standardized concentrations.

New Best Practice 24

Optimize the use of scanning machine-readable codes (e.g., barcodes and radio-frequency identification [RFID]) on patient identification (ID) bands and products to prevent medication errors.

Rationale: Barcode medication administration and other machine-readable identification technologies are important tools for preventing medication errors, but their effectiveness depends on consistent, reliable, and accurate scanning practices.

Proactively scanning barcodes on new products received by the pharmacy helps ensure end users do not encounter barcode failures during clinical workflow. Identifying unreadable, duplicate, or incorrectly configured barcodes early can prevent care interruptions and reduce reliance on unsafe workarounds.

Note: Edited excerpts from KIMSHEALTH Pharma Updates: Issue 22 and 23, KIMSHEALTH, Oman.

scramble.clue: An extremely rare inherited condition causing progressive gastrointestinal dysmotility, restricted eye movements, numbness in the hands and feet, abdominal cramps, and vomiting.
A disorder where too many mast cells accumulate in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, bone marrow, and liver, triggering a range of allergy-like symptoms.
A rare genetic disorder characterized by intellectual disability, distinctive facial features and seizures. It may be apparent at birth or become evident later in childhood.
A rare genetic disorder affecting the pancreas, bone marrow, and bones, leading to malabsorption, short stature, and skeletal abnormalities, usually presenting in childhood.
An extremely rare disease characterized by gastrointestinal polyps, hair loss, nail dystrophy and skin hyperpigmentation.
A congenital condition characterized by a small lower jaw, cleft palate, and backward displacement of the tongue.

A rare genetic condition associated with neurodevelopmental delay, varying degrees of intellectual disability, language delay, behavioural challenges, low muscle tone, a high risk of seizures and sleep difficulties.
A multisystem disorder that primarily affects the eyes, nervous system, and kidneys.
A condition characterized by craniosynostosis, facial dysmorphism, abnormalities of the hands and feet.

A rare blood disorder characterized by abnormal levels of oxidized hemoglobin that has impaired oxygen-carrying capacity and can cause bluish, purple or gray discoloration of the skin, lips, or nail beds.
A genetic disorder characterized by a sudden onset of symptoms which can be severe and life-threatening. Symptoms include nerve pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, neuropathy, and seizures.
A condition characterized by hepatic vein obstruction causing liver congestion, dysfunction, acute, subacute, or chronic liver disease, and rarely liver failure.
A rare liver disease caused by scarring, inflammation and narrowing of bile ducts, leading to liver damage and loss of its ability to filter blood and support digestion.
A group of chronic cholestasis disorders comprising a variety of genetic diseases that begin in infancy and usually progress to cirrhosis.

A progressive, genetic disorder characterized by excessive accumulation of copper in body tissues. If untreated, the excess copper can damage the liver or brain and is associated with an increased risk of liver cancer.
A rare, rapidly progressive, and fatal degenerative brain disorder causing rapid cognitive decline and memory loss.
A rare, inherited condition that causes harmful fat buildup in tissues, leading to tissue and organ damage and dysfunction.
A rare, inherited disorder that damages the myelin sheath, causing progressive loss of function of the brain and nervous system.
Inflammation of a section of the spinal cord that causes nerve damage, resulting in pain, muscle weakness, sensory problems, or bladder and bowel dysfunction.
Change in a gene that causes muscle weakness that worsens with physical activity. The muscles of the head and neck, arms and legs, and other muscles involved in movement may be affected.
